weeks.title: Your first mobile app
weeks.context:
A mobile app is not a scaled-down website. It runs on a different operating system (iOS or Android), uses different interaction paradigms (touch gestures, not clicks), has access to hardware (camera, GPS, accelerometer, biometrics), and is distributed through app stores instead of web servers. React Native bridges this gap: you write JavaScript and React, and the framework compiles to native components. This is different from a web view (showing a website inside an app shell), React Native renders real native UI components.

The project for the first 4 weeks is Hydra: a habit tracker. Simple enough to build in a weekend, complex enough to touch every foundational mobile concept, navigation, state, local storage, notifications, forms, TypeScript. By W4, Hydra is a real app that you use personally.

W1 builds Hydra v0.1: a list of habits you can check off each day. This week you understand how React Native differs from React for web. The component library is different: View instead of div, Text instead of p or h1, TouchableOpacity or Pressable instead of button. There is no CSS, styles are applied via StyleSheet objects or inline objects. StyleSheet.create is a performance optimisation that flattens style definitions at creation time. Flexbox is the only layout system (no grid, no floats, no positioning with left/top in the web sense).

Navigation is handled by a library because mobile apps do not have URLs. React Navigation is the standard. It manages a navigation stack (push and pop screens, like browser history), tab bars (bottom navigation), and drawer menus. Each screen is a React component; the navigator renders the currently active screen.

Expo is the toolchain. It provides a managed workflow that eliminates native build configuration for the first several months. The Expo Go app on your phone reads your code and renders it in real time. When you need native APIs not in Expo's managed set, you eject to a bare workflow, but stay in managed for now.

items.title: Git, version control from day 1
items.body:
## The one picture that prevents 90% of Git confusion

Git keeps your work in three places, and almost every beginner mistake comes from not knowing which one you are touching:

- **Working directory** is the files on your computer right now, exactly as you are editing them.
- **Staging area** is a holding tray for the precise changes you want in your next snapshot.
- **History** is the permanent timeline of snapshots you have already saved.

A **commit** moves changes from the staging area into history. A **push** copies that history up to GitHub so it lives somewhere other than your laptop. Every command below is just moving your work between these places. Hold this picture in your head and the commands stop feeling random.

## What Git is and why every team uses it

Git is the version-control tool behind essentially every codebase past day one. It snapshots your project after each meaningful change so you can see exactly what changed, undo a mistake without losing everything else, and work alongside other people without overwriting each other. You will use it every single day on this track, and the handful of commands below cover about 95% of daily work.

## Install Git and tell it who you are

```bash
# macOS:   brew install git
# Windows: winget install Git.Git   (or download from git-scm.com)
# Linux:   sudo apt install git

git --version
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

`git --version` prints something like `git version 2.43.0`. If you instead see `command not found`, Git is not installed yet. Install it, then reopen your terminal so the new program is found.

The two `config` lines touch no project at all. They write your identity into a settings file in your home folder so every future commit is stamped with who made it. Skip them and your very first commit dies with `Author identity unknown`.

## The five commands you will actually use

```bash
git init               # turn the current folder into a Git repo
git status             # what has changed since the last commit?
git add file.py        # move one change into the staging area
git commit -m "msg"    # save everything staged as one snapshot
git log --oneline      # the list of snapshots, newest first
```

Walk them in the order you would really use them:

- `git init` creates a hidden `.git` folder, and that folder *is* the repo. You run it once per project. It prints `Initialized empty Git repository`.
- `git status` is the command you will run most. It shows which files changed and whether they are staged yet. Run it whenever you are unsure what state you are in, because it never changes anything itself.
- `git add file.py` moves that file's changes into staging. Nothing is saved yet, you are only choosing what goes into the next snapshot. Use `git add .` to stage everything at once.
- `git commit -m "msg"` writes everything staged into history as one snapshot. The `-m` flag is your one-line note to your future self about what changed. It prints something like `1 file changed, 3 insertions(+)`.
- `git log --oneline` prints one short line per commit so you can read the trail of your work. Press `q` to leave the log view.

## Push it to GitHub so it survives your laptop

```bash
# after creating an empty repo on github.com:
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOU/your-repo.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
```

- `git remote add origin ...` saves GitHub's URL under the nickname `origin`. From here on, `origin` simply means "the GitHub copy."
- `git branch -M main` renames your current branch to `main` so it matches what GitHub expects.
- `git push -u origin main` uploads your commits to GitHub. The `-u` flag links your local `main` to GitHub's copy so that next time you can just type `git push`. Refresh the GitHub page and your files are there.

## When it breaks, and it will

- `Author identity unknown` means you skipped the two `git config` lines above. Run them, then commit again.
- `fatal: not a git repository` means you are not inside a repo folder. `cd` into the project, or run `git init` first.
- `failed to push some refs` means GitHub has a commit your laptop does not. Run `git pull` to merge it down, then push again.
- `nothing to commit, working tree clean` is not an error. Git is telling you there are no staged changes to save right now.

## Where Git shows up next

Every project on this track ships to GitHub, and every check-in you submit is backed by a commit. This is a prerequisite for everything that follows. Read it once now, and come back to it any time you are unsure which of the three places your work is currently sitting in.

items.title: What this environment is, and why before anything else
items.body:
## What it is
Mobile development needs more setup than web. You need:
1. **Node.js LTS**, same as web.
2. **Expo CLI**, `npx create-expo-app` will scaffold your projects.
3. **Expo Go** on your phone (iOS App Store / Google Play), runs your app live, no native build needed.

By the end of today you have all three. You scaffold a starter app, run `npx expo start`, scan the QR code with Expo Go on your phone, and see your app live.

## Why before anything else
Week 1 says 'create a screen and see it on your phone.' Without Expo Go set up today, that's impossible. Get it working now so the rest of the week is just code.

items.title: See it in action, the exact steps, with what you should see
items.body:
## Walkthrough
Do every step.

1. Install **Node.js LTS** from nodejs.org if you haven't already.
2. Install **Expo Go** on your phone: search 'Expo Go' on the App Store / Google Play.
3. In a terminal: `npx create-expo-app hello-forge` → confirm yes to install dependencies.
4. `cd hello-forge && npx expo start`.
5. A QR code appears in the terminal. Open Expo Go on your phone → Scan QR.
6. The starter app loads on your phone.

items.title: Zero-cost path (free alternatives)
items.body:
## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for free, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

- **Google Cloud / BigQuery**, use **DuckDB** (local, the same SQL, blazing fast) or local **Postgres**. No GCP account needed.
- **Cloud warehouse**, use **DuckDB** or local **Postgres**: identical SQL, zero cost.
- **Mobile builds**, build locally with `expo run:android` / Xcode (free); EAS cloud builds are optional, not required.

Learn the concept with the free tool; the paid service is only how some teams run it in production. The skills and the code are the same.

items.title: Why Expo + React Native?
items.body:
## A mobile app is not a scaled-down website
The foundational mindset: **a mobile app is not a scaled-down website.** It runs on a *different OS* (iOS or Android), uses *different interaction paradigms* (touch gestures, not mouse clicks), has access to *hardware* (camera, GPS, accelerometer, biometrics), and is *distributed through app stores* (not web servers). These are fundamental differences, mobile is its own platform with its own paradigms, constraints, and capabilities, not "a website on a phone." **React Native** bridges the gap for you: you write *JavaScript and React* (which you may know), and the framework *compiles to native components*. Crucially, this is *different from a web view* (showing a website inside an app shell), React Native renders *real native UI components* (a real native button, not an HTML button styled to look like one), so the app *is* a genuine native app, built with JavaScript/React.

## React Native: real native UI from JavaScript/React
Understanding *what React Native is* (and isn't) frames the whole track:
- **You write React, it renders native:** you use *React* (components, state, props, the component model from web React) and *JavaScript*, and React Native *translates* your components into *real native UI components* (iOS's and Android's actual native views). So your React `<View>` becomes a native view, your `<Text>` a native text element. You get to use *familiar* React (if you know it from web) to build *genuinely native* mobile UI.
- **It's not a web view (a key distinction):** a *web view* approach (Cordova/older hybrid apps) shows a *website* inside an app wrapper, the UI is HTML rendered in a browser inside the app, which *feels* non-native (it's a web page). React Native is *fundamentally different*: it renders *real native components*, so the app *looks and feels native* (native scrolling, native controls, native performance) because it *is* using the native UI. This is why React Native apps can feel like real native apps, they *are* native UI, driven by your JavaScript/React.
- **Cross-platform from one codebase:** you write *one* React Native codebase and it runs on *both* iOS and Android (rendering native components on each), so you build for both platforms from one codebase, a major productivity advantage over writing separate native apps. (You handle platform differences where needed, but much is shared.)
So React Native lets you build *real, native, cross-platform* mobile apps using *JavaScript and React*, rendering *actual native UI* (not a web view), which is the foundation of this track.

## What you'll build: Hydra
The project for the first 4 weeks is **Hydra: a habit tracker**, *simple* enough to build in a weekend, *complex* enough to touch *every foundational mobile concept*, navigation, state, local storage, notifications, forms, TypeScript. By W4, Hydra is a *real app you use personally*. This week builds **Hydra v0.1**: a list of habits you can tap to mark complete, with the progress saved locally. Building Hydra teaches the core of mobile development hands-on (the same project-driven, ship-each-version approach as the other tracks' capstones, FlightWise, Bean Forge), and growing *one* app from v0.1 to a real, polished, store-shipped app (by the track's end) is how you learn mobile development by *doing*.

## Where this fits
This opens the **Foundations phase** (W1-4): building Hydra (a habit tracker) from a simple v0.1 to a TypeScript, history-tracking, notification-sending real app, learning the core mobile concepts (React Native, state, local storage, notifications, TypeScript) hands-on. It's the foundation for the whole track (screens, native integration, backend, polish, distribution). Today's orientation: a mobile app is its own platform (not a scaled-down website), and React Native lets you build *real, native, cross-platform* apps from *JavaScript/React* (rendering real native UI, not a web view), which you'll learn by building Hydra. Tomorrow you set up the tools: Node and Expo Go.

items.title: Install Node.js and Expo Go
items.body:
## Set up with Expo: the easy path to React Native
You build with **Expo**, the framework/toolchain that makes React Native development *dramatically* easier, and **Expo Go**, the app that lets you *run your app on your real phone instantly* while developing. Setup is straightforward:
```bash
# install Node.js (the JS runtime, as for web)
npx create-expo-app hydra      # scaffold a new Expo (React Native) app
cd hydra
npx expo start                 # start the dev server -> scan the QR code with Expo Go on your phone
```
You install **Expo Go** (a free app) on your phone, run `expo start`, scan the QR code, and your app *runs on your actual phone*, with *live reload* (save code, see it update on the phone instantly). This is a magical developer experience: you're developing a real mobile app and seeing it on your real device immediately, no complex native build setup.

## Why Expo, and what it gives you
Understanding *why* Expo (vs raw React Native) is the recommended path frames the toolchain:
- **It removes the painful native setup:** raw React Native development requires setting up native toolchains (Xcode for iOS, Android Studio for Android), which is complex and platform-dependent (you need a Mac for iOS, lots of configuration). *Expo* abstracts most of this away, you develop in JavaScript with `expo start` and *Expo Go*, *without* needing the native toolchains for most development, which is a *huge* reduction in setup friction (especially valuable for getting started, and for developing iOS apps without a Mac). Expo makes React Native *accessible*.
- **Expo Go for instant on-device development:** *Expo Go* lets you run your app on your *real phone* (or simulator) *instantly* by scanning a QR code, with *live reload*, so your develop-test loop is *fast* (change code, see it on your phone immediately). This instant, on-real-device feedback is a fantastic developer experience and makes mobile development feel *immediate* (vs the slow build-deploy cycles of raw native development).
- **Expo SDK: native capabilities made easy:** Expo provides a rich *SDK* of pre-built modules for *native capabilities* (camera, notifications, location, storage, etc., the native integrations in later weeks), so you access device hardware/features through *easy JavaScript APIs* (expo-camera, expo-notifications, expo-location, etc.) *without* writing native code. This makes the native integrations (W9-12) far easier than raw React Native. Expo gives you native capabilities through simple JS.
- **EAS for building/shipping:** Expo also provides *EAS* (Expo Application Services) for *building* and *submitting* your app to the stores (W21), handling the native build process in the cloud. So Expo covers the whole lifecycle, develop (Expo Go), access native features (SDK), and build/ship (EAS).
So Expo is the recommended path because it *removes the painful native setup* (develop in JS without Xcode/Android Studio for most work), provides *instant on-device development* (Expo Go + live reload), makes *native capabilities easy* (the Expo SDK), and handles *building/shipping* (EAS), dramatically lowering the barrier to building real React Native apps.

## The modern Expo workflow
The practical workflow you're setting up is the *modern* Expo development flow, which is how most React Native apps are built today. You *develop* in JavaScript/React with `expo start` and *Expo Go* (instant on-device, live reload), using *Expo SDK* modules for native features, and when you need a *custom* native module not in the SDK (rarer), Expo's *development builds* / config plugins let you add native code while keeping the Expo workflow (the "you're not locked out of native" point, relevant to W12). When ready to *ship*, you use *EAS Build* to produce the native app binaries and *EAS Submit* to send them to the stores (W21). This Expo-centric workflow, develop in JS with Expo Go, native features via the SDK, build/ship via EAS, is the *standard, recommended* way to build React Native apps now (vs the more complex raw React Native CLI workflow), because it gives you *most* of the power of React Native with *far less* of the native-setup friction. You're setting up this workflow now, and it's the foundation for everything: you'll develop Hydra (and beyond) in this fast, accessible, on-device JavaScript loop, accessing native features through Expo's SDK, and eventually ship via EAS. Getting comfortable with the Expo workflow (the dev server, Expo Go on your phone, live reload, the SDK) is the practical foundation for productive mobile development on this track. The fact that you can build a real native app, running on your real phone, in JavaScript, with this little setup, is exactly the accessibility Expo provides.

## Where this fits
You set up the Expo workflow: Node, `create-expo-app`, `expo start`, and *Expo Go* running your app on your real phone with live reload, the modern, accessible React Native toolchain that removes painful native setup, provides instant on-device development, makes native capabilities easy (the Expo SDK), and handles building/shipping (EAS). Tomorrow you start building Hydra's UI with React components.

items.title: Tap to fill, useState
items.body:
## Interactivity with state: tap to fill
You make Hydra interactive with **state**, exactly the `useState` from web React, now driving native UI. The core Hydra interaction: tap a glass to "fill" it (mark that water intake), which updates state, which re-renders the UI:
```jsx
function Hydra() {
  const [filled, setFilled] = useState(0);          // how many glasses filled today
  const goal = 8;
  return (
    <View>
      <Text>{filled} / {goal} glasses</Text>
      {Array.from({ length: goal }).map((_, i) => (
        <Glass key={i} filled={i < filled} onPress={() => setFilled(filled + 1)} />
      ))}
    </View>
  );
}
```
`useState` holds the count of filled glasses, tapping a glass calls `setFilled` to increment it, and React *re-renders* to show the updated count and filled glasses, the *same* state-and-render-loop from web React (state changes -> re-render -> UI updates), now in a native mobile app. Tapping the glasses *feels* native (real touch on real native components) while being driven by the React state model you know.

## The same React state model, on mobile
The key realisation is that *state works identically* to web React, which means your state knowledge transfers completely:
- **`useState` and the render loop are the same:** you use `useState` to hold changeable data, call the setter to update it, and React re-renders the (native) UI to match, *exactly* as on web. The "UI as a function of state", change state, React updates the UI, is identical; only the *components* being rendered are native (instead of HTML). So Hydra's interactivity (tap to fill, the count updates) is the *same* declarative state-driven model you know, you're not learning a new interactivity model, just applying the React one to native UI.
- **All the state rules transfer:** immutable updates (use the setter, don't mutate state directly), lifting state up (when shared), the categories of state, *all* the state knowledge from web React applies on mobile. State management on React Native is React state management.
- **Touch events drive state changes:** the difference is that state changes are triggered by *touch* (`onPress`) instead of clicks, but the pattern (an interaction handler calls a state setter, triggering a re-render) is identical. Tap -> `setFilled` -> re-render is the mobile version of click -> `setState` -> re-render.
So Hydra's interactivity, and *all* React Native interactivity, uses the *same* React state model you know (`useState`, the render loop, immutable updates, lifting state), now driving *native* UI in response to *touch*. Your web React state knowledge transfers directly, which is a major part of why React Native is accessible to React developers.

## Building real interactivity, the mobile way
As you build Hydra's tap-to-fill interaction, you're practising the core loop of mobile app interactivity, which is the React state model applied to native, touch-driven UI. The pattern, *touch triggers a state change, which re-renders the native UI*, is how *all* interactive mobile features work (tapping, toggling, navigating, all are touch -> state change -> re-render), so mastering it on Hydra's simple tap-to-fill is mastering the foundation of mobile interactivity. You'll layer on mobile-specific interaction richness later (gestures, animations, W6), but the *foundation* is this React state model driven by touch, which you already know from web React, now native. The progression, build native UI (D3), make it interactive with state (today), persist it (tomorrow), is the same build-an-interactive-app arc, in the mobile context. Hydra is becoming a *real interactive app*: native UI (the glasses), interactive via state (tap to fill, the count updates), all in the familiar React model. The takeaway is that *mobile interactivity is React state management driving native, touch-driven UI*, so your React knowledge gives you the interactivity model directly, and you build mobile features by applying it (touch handlers calling state setters, re-rendering native components). This foundation makes the rest of the track's interactive features (forms, gestures, navigation, all the screens) approachable, because they're all built on this same state-and-touch model you're learning now on Hydra.

## Where this fits
You can build mobile interactivity with React state: `useState` and the render loop (identical to web React) driving *native* UI in response to *touch* (`onPress`), so Hydra's tap-to-fill works via the familiar change-state-and-re-render model, and all your React state knowledge transfers. Hydra is now interactive. Tomorrow you make it persist with AsyncStorage.

days.summary: Right now if you close the app, progress is lost. Today we fix that.

items.title: Save progress, AsyncStorage
items.body:
## Persistence: saving progress with AsyncStorage
Hydra's progress vanishes when you close the app (state is in memory, lost on close), so you add **persistence** with **AsyncStorage**, React Native's simple *key-value storage* for saving data *on the device*, the mobile equivalent of web's localStorage:
```jsx
import AsyncStorage from '@react-native-async-storage/async-storage';
// save (AsyncStorage is async - it returns promises):
await AsyncStorage.setItem('filled', String(filled));
// load (e.g. on app start):
const saved = await AsyncStorage.getItem('filled');   // null if not set
if (saved !== null) setFilled(Number(saved));
```
You *save* the filled count whenever it changes, and *load* it when the app starts, so Hydra *remembers* your progress across app restarts. AsyncStorage persists data *on the device* (it survives app closes/restarts), giving Hydra the persistence a real daily-use app needs.

## AsyncStorage: the mobile key-value store
Understanding AsyncStorage (and its nature) is foundational mobile persistence knowledge:
- **It's device-local key-value storage (like localStorage):** AsyncStorage stores *string* key-value pairs *on the device*, persisting across app sessions, *conceptually like web's localStorage* (which you know). You `setItem(key, value)` and `getItem(key)`, storing strings (so you `JSON.stringify`/`JSON.parse` objects, and convert numbers, as with localStorage). It's the *simple, default* way to persist small data on the device.
- **It's *asynchronous* (the key difference from localStorage):** unlike web's *synchronous* localStorage, AsyncStorage is *asynchronous* (its methods return *promises*, you `await` them), because mobile storage I/O is async. So you use `await` (or `.then`) with AsyncStorage, and handle the async nature (e.g. loading saved data is an async operation you do on startup, often in a `useEffect`). This async nature is a small but important difference, AsyncStorage operations are async I/O, not instant.
- **It's for *simple* data:** AsyncStorage is *good* for *simple* data, settings, preferences, small state (like Hydra's filled count, the reminder time later), the kind of small key-value data localStorage handles on web. It's the right tool for *simple* persistence, and you'll see its *limits* for *structured/queryable* data soon (W3, where you'll reach for SQLite), but for *simple* device-local persistence, AsyncStorage is the easy, standard choice.
So AsyncStorage is React Native's *simple, device-local, async key-value store* (like an async localStorage), the standard tool for persisting *simple* data (settings, small state) on the device across sessions, which is exactly what Hydra v0.1 needs to *remember* your progress.

## Persistence makes it a real app, and the mobile data picture
The deeper point is that *persistence is what makes Hydra a *real*, daily-use app* (it remembers your progress), and AsyncStorage is your first tool in the *mobile data-persistence picture* that the track develops. An app that *forgets* everything on close isn't useful for a habit tracker (your progress must persist day to day), so *persistence* is essential, and AsyncStorage provides it simply for Hydra's small state. This is the mobile version of the persistence you saw on web (localStorage), with the same role (remember data across sessions) and the same simple-key-value nature (plus the async difference). As Hydra grows (W3's history/streaks need *structured* data), you'll feel AsyncStorage's *limits* (it's awkward for structured, queryable data) and reach for *SQLite* (W3) and learn the *full* mobile storage picture (AsyncStorage for simple data, SQLite for structured, MMKV for fast key-value, W8), but you *start* with AsyncStorage for *simple* persistence, which is the right first tool. The takeaway is that *mobile apps need device-local persistence* (to remember data across sessions), AsyncStorage is the *simple* tool for it (async key-value, like localStorage), and using it (save on change, load on startup, handle the async nature) is how you make Hydra *remember*, turning it from a session-only toy into a *real* app that retains your progress. This foundational persistence (and the awareness that richer storage tools come later for richer needs) is essential mobile knowledge, and it's what makes Hydra v0.1 a genuinely usable daily app.

## Where this fits
You can persist data with AsyncStorage: React Native's simple, device-local, *async* key-value store (like an async localStorage), used to save Hydra's progress (set on change, load on startup) so it *remembers* across sessions, the right tool for *simple* data (with SQLite and MMKV coming later for structured/fast needs). Hydra now persists. Tomorrow you polish its look.

items.title: Polish the look
items.body:
## Polish the look: making Hydra feel good
With Hydra functional (native UI, interactive, persistent), you *polish its look* so it *feels* like a real, pleasant app, applying styling and design care via StyleSheet and Flexbox. Good mobile visual polish includes:
```text
- consistent spacing and sizing (a spacing scale, generous touch targets)
- a cohesive color palette (Hydra's water-blue theme)
- good typography (readable sizes, sensible hierarchy)
- proper layout (Flexbox, centered/balanced, respecting safe areas - notches, status bars)
- visual feedback on touch (the glass visibly fills, pressables respond)
- attention to the mobile context (it looks right on a real phone screen)
```
You refine Hydra's styling, consistent colors and spacing, good typography, balanced Flexbox layout, clear touch feedback, so it looks *designed* and *polished*, not rough. This is the same design-system/consistency discipline from web (consistent palette and spacing produce a designed look), applied to mobile UI.

## Mobile-specific visual considerations
Mobile polish has *specific* considerations beyond general design that are worth knowing:
- **Touch targets must be big enough:** interactive elements (buttons, the glasses) must be *large enough to tap comfortably* with a finger (a minimum tap size, ~44pt), unlike a precise mouse cursor, fingers are imprecise, so mobile touch targets must be *generously sized* and *well-spaced* (so you don't mis-tap). This is a key mobile-specific design rule, design for fingers, not cursors.
- **Safe areas (notches, status bars, home indicators):** modern phones have *notches*, *status bars*, *rounded corners*, and *home indicators* that your UI must *avoid* (don't put content under the notch or behind the home indicator), so you respect *safe areas* (using `SafeAreaView` / safe-area insets) to keep content in the usable screen region. This is a mobile-specific layout concern, the screen isn't a clean rectangle; you design around the device's safe area.
- **Responsive to different screen sizes:** phones vary in size, so (like responsive web) your layout should *adapt* (Flexbox helps, plus avoiding fixed sizes that break on small/large screens), so Hydra looks good on different phones. Mobile responsiveness is about the range of phone sizes.
- **Platform feel (iOS vs Android):** iOS and Android have *different* design conventions (navigation patterns, controls, typography), and a polished app *respects* the platform's feel (or has a cohesive cross-platform design), so it feels *native* on each. You're at least aware that the platforms have different conventions.
So mobile polish includes the *mobile-specific* considerations, generous touch targets (for fingers), respecting safe areas (notches/bars), responsiveness to phone sizes, and platform feel, on top of general visual design (consistent palette, spacing, typography). Attending to these is what makes a mobile app feel *properly* designed *for mobile*, not just a generic UI.

## Why polish matters (the mobile-app-quality bar)
The deeper point, echoing the web track's polish theme, is that *mobile users have high expectations for app quality and polish*, perhaps even *higher* than web, because mobile apps are held to the standard of the *highly-polished* apps users use daily (the bar set by professional iOS/Android apps), so a rough-feeling mobile app stands out as *amateur* immediately. Mobile users *notice* polish (smooth interactions, good touch feedback, proper layout, consistent design) and *reject* roughness (tiny touch targets, content under the notch, janky layout, inconsistent design) quickly, the app-store world is full of polished apps, so quality is *expected*. So polishing Hydra's look (consistent design, proper touch targets, safe areas, responsiveness, clear feedback) isn't optional nicety; it's part of meeting the *quality bar* that mobile users expect and that distinguishes a *real* app from a rough prototype. This is the same "polish is what users notice / separates product from side project" lesson from web (W23), with the mobile-specific bar (and considerations) on top. Building the habit *now* (v0.1) of polishing the look, with attention to the mobile-specific details (touch targets, safe areas, feel), sets the right standard for everything you'll build, and it's what makes Hydra feel like a *real* app you'd want to use. Mobile polish, general design plus mobile-specific care, is essential to meeting users' high app-quality expectations.

## Where this fits
You polished Hydra's look: consistent design (palette, spacing, typography) via StyleSheet/Flexbox, plus the mobile-specific considerations, generous touch targets (for fingers), respecting safe areas (notches/bars), responsiveness to phone sizes, and platform feel, meeting the high app-quality bar mobile users expect. Hydra looks like a real app. Tomorrow you build it into an installable APK and ship it.

items.title: Build the APK and ship
items.body:
## Build the APK and ship Hydra v0.1
You make Hydra a *real, installable app* by building an **APK** (the Android app package) and getting it onto a phone, the mobile equivalent of deploying. With Expo's **EAS Build**, you build the app binary in the cloud (no local native toolchain needed):
```bash
eas build --platform android --profile preview    # builds an installable APK in the cloud
# -> download the APK and install it on an Android phone (or share it)
```
EAS Build compiles your React Native/Expo app into a *real native binary* (an APK for Android) that you can *install on a phone* (and share), so Hydra v0.1 becomes a *real, installed app* (not just running in Expo Go). This is shipping for mobile, producing an installable app artifact. (Full *store* submission comes in W21; here you build an installable APK to have a real, shippable v0.1.)

## Why building a real binary matters
Understanding *why* building the real installable app (vs just running in Expo Go) matters frames the milestone:
- **It's a *real* app, not just dev mode:** running in *Expo Go* (development) is great for *building*, but it's running *inside* the Expo Go app (dev mode), not as a *standalone* app. *Building* (EAS Build) produces a *real, standalone, installable* app (the APK), Hydra as its *own* installed app on the phone, which is the *real* artifact. So building turns your dev project into a *genuine installable app*, the difference between "it runs in Expo Go on my machine" and "it's a real app installed on a phone."
- **EAS Build handles the native build (in the cloud):** building a native app normally requires the native toolchains (Xcode/Android Studio) and complex configuration, but *EAS Build* does it *in the cloud* (Expo's servers build the binary), so you get a real native build *without* the local native-build setup (consistent with Expo's remove-the-native-friction theme). This makes *shipping* a real app accessible, you run one command and get an installable binary.
- **It's the path to the stores:** building an installable app (now) is the foundation for *store submission* (W21, where you build for both stores and submit via EAS), so this is your first step on the *distribution* path, producing a real app binary, which you'll later submit to the app stores. Building the APK now is shipping v0.1 *and* learning the build process you'll use to reach the stores.
So building the APK matters because it produces a *real, standalone, installable* app (not just dev-mode Expo Go), via EAS Build's cloud native build (no local toolchain needed), which is your first real "ship" for mobile and the foundation for store distribution. Hydra v0.1 is now a *real app on a real phone*.

## Ship v0.1, and the Hydra journey begins
You ship Hydra v0.1, version it, and begin the project's journey (the same ship-each-version discipline as the other tracks):
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Hydra v0.1: tap-to-fill habit tracker (React Native + Expo)"
git tag v0.1
git push
# + the built APK installed on your phone - a real app you use
```
Hydra v0.1 is a *real, installed, used* app: native UI (the glasses), interactive (tap to fill), persistent (remembers progress), polished (looks good), and *built into an installable APK on your phone*. You'll grow it (v0.2 notifications, v0.3 history/streaks, v0.4 TypeScript) into a real daily-use app, tagging each version, building the project history that demonstrates a *growing, shipped* app. The takeaway from v0.1: you've built and shipped a *real native mobile app*, from React/JavaScript, using Expo, the foundational accomplishment that proves you can build mobile apps, and the *ship-it* habit (build the real artifact, get it on a phone, version it) that you'll repeat throughout. Hydra v0.1 on your phone is the concrete proof that you can build real mobile apps, and the beginning of the project that carries the whole track.

## Where this fits
You built Hydra v0.1 into a real, installable APK (via EAS Build's cloud native build) and shipped it, a real, standalone, installed mobile app on your phone (not just Expo Go dev mode), the first "ship" for mobile and the foundation for store distribution (W21). Hydra v0.1 is real and used. Next week you grow it: **Hydra v0.2** adds a *daily reset* and *reminder notifications* (local notifications scheduled by the OS), introducing the notifications and scheduled-work APIs that are fundamentally mobile, making Hydra a true daily-use app.

weeks.title: Hydra v0.2: Daily reset + reminder notification
weeks.context:
Hydra v0.2 adds two features that make it a real daily-use app: a daily reset (habits reset to unchecked at midnight) and reminder notifications (push a local notification at a user-configured time to prompt the daily check-in). These features introduce the local notifications API and scheduled background work, two things that are fundamentally different on mobile vs web.

Local notifications are scheduled by your app and delivered by the operating system. They do not require a server, a push notification service, or network connectivity. They are just a request to the OS: "at 8am every morning, show this notification." The OS delivers it even if the app is not running. expo-notifications is the library that handles this. You request permission first (required on iOS, optional on Android) and then schedule the notification.

Notification permissions are granted by the user. On iOS, the permission dialog appears the first time you request it, if the user denies, you cannot ask again programmatically (they must enable manually in Settings). This means you should explain why you need permission before requesting it. Show a prompt: "Hydra sends you a daily reminder at your chosen time. Tap Allow to enable notifications." If they tap Allow, then you call the permission request.

Date and time handling is harder than it looks on mobile. The user's time zone matters: a reminder at 8am should fire at 8am in the user's local time, not 8am UTC. The daily reset at midnight must use the device's local midnight, not UTC midnight. Use the device's local time for all scheduling. expo-notifications handles this correctly when you use Calendar triggers with local time.

AsyncStorage is the simplest form of local persistence, a key-value store backed by the device's file system. Think of it as localStorage for React Native. You store the reminder time and whether the user has configured it. AsyncStorage is asynchronous (it reads from disk), always await it and handle the case where the value is null (first launch).

items.title: What we're adding
items.body:
## Making Hydra a real daily-use app
Hydra v0.2 adds two features that turn it from a toy into a *real daily-use* app: a **daily reset** (habits reset to unchecked at midnight, so each day is fresh) and **reminder notifications** (a local notification at a user-chosen time, prompting the daily check-in). These introduce two things that are *fundamentally different on mobile than on web*: the **local notifications API** and **scheduled background work**, capabilities the OS provides that web apps largely can't match. This week you make Hydra prompt you daily (so you actually use it) and reset each day (so it tracks *daily* habits), the features that make a habit tracker genuinely useful day to day.

## Local notifications: the OS works for you
The headline new capability is **local notifications**, notifications your app *schedules* and the *operating system delivers*, even when your app isn't running:
```text
your app:  "OS, at 12pm every day, show this notification: 'Time to hydrate!'"
the OS:    delivers it at 12pm daily - EVEN IF the app is closed/not running
```
The crucial properties: local notifications are *scheduled by your app* but *delivered by the OS*, they *don't* require a server, a push-notification service, or network connectivity (unlike *remote* push notifications, W11), they're *just a request to the OS* ("show this at this time"). And the OS delivers them *even if your app isn't running*, which is the key, the OS does the work for you, on schedule, regardless of your app's state. `expo-notifications` is the library that handles this: you *request permission* first (required on iOS, optional on Android), then *schedule* the notification. This is a fundamentally *mobile* capability, the OS delivering scheduled notifications for your app, that enables the "remind me daily" habit-tracker behavior.

## Why this is fundamentally mobile (and different from web)
Understanding *why* notifications and scheduled work are fundamentally mobile frames the week:
- **The OS delivers them even when your app isn't running:** the defining mobile capability is that the *operating system* delivers your scheduled notification *regardless of your app's state* (closed, backgrounded), the OS is *working for you* on schedule. A *web* page generally *can't* do this (a closed browser tab can't show a notification on a schedule), so this OS-delivered, app-not-running scheduled notification is a distinctly *mobile* (native-platform) power. It's why a mobile habit tracker can *reliably* remind you daily (the OS guarantees the delivery) in a way a web app can't.
- **No server/network needed (local notifications):** *local* notifications need *no server, no push service, no network*, they're entirely *on-device* (your app tells the OS, the OS delivers locally). This is simpler and more reliable than *remote* push (W11, which needs a server and network), for a *scheduled local reminder* (like Hydra's daily prompt), local notifications are perfect, requiring nothing but the app and the OS. (Remote push, for server-triggered notifications, is W11.)
- **Permissions matter (mobile's user-consent model):** mobile OSes *gate* powerful capabilities (notifications, and later camera, location, etc.) behind *user permission*, you must *request* permission (and the user must *grant* it), which is a core *mobile* concept (the OS protects the user by requiring consent for capabilities). For notifications, you request permission *first* (required on iOS), and handle the case where it's *denied* (the user said no, so you can't send notifications, you handle that gracefully). This permission model is fundamental to mobile, you ask for capabilities, the user grants or denies, and you respect that.
So local notifications (and scheduled work) are *fundamentally mobile* because the *OS delivers them even when your app isn't running* (a power web lacks), they need *no server/network* (local, on-device), and they involve the *mobile permission model* (request consent for capabilities). These OS-level, app-state-independent capabilities are part of what makes mobile apps powerful and distinct from web.

## Where this fits
This week grows Hydra to v0.2 with a daily reset and reminder notifications, introducing *local notifications* (OS-delivered, scheduled, no-server) and *scheduled background work*, fundamentally mobile capabilities (the OS works for you even when the app's closed), plus the mobile *permission* model. It's a step toward Hydra being a real daily-use app. Today's orientation: local notifications (scheduled by your app, delivered by the OS even when the app isn't running, no server needed) and the permission model are fundamentally mobile, and they make Hydra able to remind you daily. Tomorrow you handle the daily reset (storing today's date with the state).

items.body:
## Installing and setting up notifications
You add reminder notifications using **expo-notifications**, the Expo library for local (and later remote) notifications. Setup involves installing it and, crucially, *requesting permission*:
```bash
npx expo install expo-notifications
```
```jsx
import * as Notifications from 'expo-notifications';
// request permission (required on iOS):
const { status } = await Notifications.requestPermissionsAsync();
if (status !== 'granted') {
  // the user denied - handle gracefully (can't send notifications)
}
```
You install the library and *request notification permission* from the user, and you *handle the result*, if *granted*, you can schedule notifications (tomorrow); if *denied*, you *cannot*, so you handle that case (don't crash, maybe inform the user notifications are off). Requesting and handling permission is the *first*, *required* step before any notification work.

## The permission model: a core mobile concept
Understanding mobile *permissions* (introduced here, recurring for every native capability) is essential mobile knowledge:
- **The OS gates capabilities behind user consent:** mobile OSes *protect users* by requiring *explicit permission* for powerful/sensitive capabilities, notifications, camera, location, contacts, etc. Your app *cannot* use these without the user *granting* permission, the OS *asks* the user (shows a permission dialog) and your app gets the result (granted/denied). This *consent model* is fundamental to mobile, capabilities are *opt-in* by the user, which protects user privacy/control, and your app must *work within* it (request permission, respect the answer).
- **You must request, handle all outcomes, and respect denial:** for *each* capability, you *request* permission (`requestPermissionsAsync`), and you *handle all outcomes*, *granted* (proceed), *denied* (you *can't* use the capability, so degrade gracefully, don't crash, maybe explain or offer settings), and *undetermined/ask-again*. Crucially, you *respect* denial, if the user says no, you *don't* (can't) use the capability, and your app should still *work* (without that feature) rather than break. So handling permissions means requesting, handling grant *and* denial, and respecting the user's choice. (Denied is a *real, common* case you must handle, not an edge case.)
- **Request at the right time, with context:** best practice is to request a permission *when it's relevant* (when the user is about to use the feature, so they understand *why*) and ideally with *context* (explain *why* you need it), rather than blasting all permission requests at app launch (which users reflexively deny). For Hydra's notifications, you'd request when the user *enables* reminders (in the settings screen, D5), so the request makes sense to them. Requesting permissions *contextually* (when relevant, with reason) gets more *grants* and respects the user, a UX-and-consent best practice.
So the permission model, the OS gates capabilities behind *user consent*, you *request* permission and *handle all outcomes* (granted, *and gracefully* denied), *respect* the user's choice, and *request contextually* (when relevant, with reason), is a *core mobile concept* you meet here with notifications and apply to *every* native capability (camera, location, etc., the W9-12 integrations). Internalising it now (request, handle grant/denial gracefully, respect denial, ask contextually) sets the pattern for all native-capability work.

## Why permissions matter (privacy, trust, robustness)
The deeper significance is that the *permission model embodies mobile's user-privacy-and-control ethos*, and handling it well is both *required* and *respectful*. Mobile platforms put the *user in control* of their device's capabilities (the user decides whether an app can send notifications, access the camera, know their location), which *protects user privacy and trust*, and your app *must* work within this (you *can't* just take these capabilities; the user grants them). Handling permissions *well*, requesting *contextually* (so users understand and are more likely to grant), handling *denial gracefully* (the app still works without the feature), and *respecting* the user's choice (not nagging or breaking), is part of building a *trustworthy, robust* app that *respects users* (the user-respect theme from across the tracks, here enforced by the platform). It's also *robustness*, you *must* handle the denied case (it *will* happen), or your app breaks for users who decline. So the permission model isn't just a technical step; it's mobile's *privacy-and-consent* framework that you work within respectfully and robustly. For Hydra, you request notification permission (to send reminders), handle if the user declines (Hydra still works, just without reminders), and request it at the right moment (when they enable reminders). Getting permissions right, request, handle all outcomes, respect the user, ask contextually, is foundational to building real, respectful, robust mobile apps, and you establish the pattern here with notifications.

## Where this fits
You installed expo-notifications and learned the *permission model*, the OS gates capabilities (notifications, camera, location...) behind *user consent*, so you *request* permission and *handle all outcomes* (granted, and gracefully denied), *respect* the user's choice, and *request contextually* (when relevant, with reason), a core mobile concept embodying mobile's privacy-and-control ethos, applied to every native capability. Tomorrow you schedule the reminder notification.

items.title: Notification permission
Schedule a 12pm reminder
items.body:
## Scheduling the reminder notification
With permission granted, you *schedule* the daily reminder, a local notification the OS delivers at the user's chosen time, every day:
```jsx
await Notifications.scheduleNotificationAsync({
  content: { title: 'Time to hydrate!', body: "Don't forget your water today." },
  trigger: { hour: 12, minute: 0, repeats: true },   // 12pm every day
});
```
You give the notification's *content* (title, body) and a *trigger* (when to fire, here 12pm daily, `repeats: true` for every day), and the OS *schedules* it, delivering "Time to hydrate!" at 12pm *every day*, even when Hydra is closed. You also *manage* scheduled notifications, *cancel* the old one when the user *changes* the reminder time (so you don't stack duplicates), reschedule with the new time. This gives Hydra its daily reminder, the OS prompting the user to check in.

## How scheduling works, and managing notifications
Understanding the scheduling API and its management completes the local-notification picture:
- **Schedule with content + trigger:** you specify *what* (content, the title/body the user sees) and *when* (trigger, a time, an interval, daily-repeating, etc.), and the OS handles *delivering* it on that schedule. For Hydra, a *daily-repeating* trigger at the chosen hour gives the daily reminder. The API is simple, describe the notification and its schedule, the OS does the rest.
- **Manage the scheduled notifications (avoid duplicates):** scheduled notifications *persist* (the OS keeps delivering them until canceled), so you must *manage* them, when the user *changes* the reminder time, you *cancel* the existing scheduled notification and *schedule* a new one (else you'd have *both*, duplicate reminders). So you track/cancel and reschedule as settings change. Managing the scheduled notification set (cancel old, schedule new on change) keeps it correct (one reminder at the right time, not stacking duplicates). (`cancelAllScheduledNotificationsAsync` or canceling by ID, then rescheduling.)
- **The notification fires even when the app is closed:** the key property (D1), once scheduled, the OS delivers it *regardless of the app's state*, so the daily reminder *works* even if Hydra hasn't been opened, the OS reliably prompts the user. This is the local-notification power, schedule once, the OS delivers on schedule indefinitely (until canceled), independent of your app running.
So you schedule the reminder by specifying *content* and a *daily-repeating trigger*, the OS delivers it daily (even when the app's closed), and you *manage* the scheduled notifications (cancel and reschedule when the time changes) to keep it correct (no duplicates). This gives Hydra a reliable daily reminder via the OS.

## Why local notifications are powerful for engagement
The deeper point is that *local notifications are a powerful, simple tool for app engagement*, prompting the user to *return* to and *use* the app, which is especially valuable for a *habit* app (whose whole point is daily use). A habit tracker *needs* to *remind* the user to engage daily (or they forget and the habit, and the app's value, lapses), and local notifications provide exactly that, a reliable daily prompt, *for free* (no server, just the OS), that brings the user back. This *re-engagement* is a major reason mobile apps use notifications (the daily prompt that drives habitual use), and *local* notifications (scheduled, on-device) are the *simple* version (perfect for Hydra's "remind me at this time" need), while *remote* push (W11) handles server-triggered, dynamic notifications. For Hydra, the local daily reminder is *core* to its value, it's what makes Hydra a *habit-forming* app (it prompts you to hydrate daily) rather than one you forget to open. Using local notifications well, scheduled reliably, managed correctly, *respectful* (the user chose the time, can disable them, the consent/respect theme), is a key mobile skill for engagement. The discipline is to use notifications to *genuinely help* the user (a useful, wanted reminder, like Hydra's hydration prompt) rather than to *spam/annoy* (excessive, unwanted notifications, which users disable or uninstall over), so you send *valuable, user-chosen* notifications respectfully. Hydra's well-scheduled, user-configured, respectful daily reminder exemplifies using local notifications to *help* the user engage, which is what makes it a real daily-use app. Local notifications, used respectfully for genuine value, are a powerful engagement tool, and Hydra's reminder shows it.

## Where this fits
You schedule Hydra's daily reminder, a local notification (content + daily-repeating trigger) the OS delivers daily even when the app's closed, managed correctly (cancel and reschedule when the time changes, no duplicates), giving Hydra a reliable, OS-delivered daily prompt, a powerful, simple, respectful engagement tool that makes it a real habit app. Tomorrow you build a settings screen so the user can configure the reminder.

items.title: Add a settings screen
items.body:
## A settings screen: configuring the reminder
The reminder time should be *user-configurable*, so you build a **settings screen** where the user sets their reminder time (and toggles reminders on/off), which introduces *navigation* (moving between screens) and *more complex forms/inputs*:
```text
settings screen:  - a toggle to enable/disable reminders
                  - a time picker to choose the reminder time
                  - (changing these reschedules/cancels the notification, D4)
navigation:       move from the main screen to the settings screen and back
```
You add a *settings screen* (separate from the main Hydra screen) with a *reminder toggle* and a *time picker*, and *navigation* to move between the main and settings screens. When the user changes the setting, you *update* the scheduled notification (reschedule/cancel, D4) and *persist* the preference (AsyncStorage). This makes the reminder *user-controlled* (they choose if and when), which is essential (a fixed, non-configurable reminder is much worse).

## Navigation: moving between screens
The new concept is **navigation**, how mobile apps move between *screens*, a core mobile pattern:
- **Mobile apps are organized into screens, with navigation between them:** unlike a single-page web view, mobile apps are typically *multiple screens* (main, settings, detail, etc.) with *navigation* between them (push a screen, go back, switch tabs). *Navigation* is how the user *moves* through the app's screens, and it's a *fundamental* mobile structure. **React Navigation** (or Expo Router) is the standard library for this, providing *navigators* (stack navigator for push/back, tab navigator for tabs) that manage the screens and transitions.
- **Stack navigation (push/back) is the basic pattern:** the most common is the *stack* navigator, screens are *pushed* onto a stack (navigate to settings -> settings pushes on top) and *popped* (back -> settings pops off, returning to main), with native push/back *transitions* and a *back gesture/button*. This *stack* model (push a screen, go back) is the core navigation pattern, and it *feels native* (the native push animation, swipe-back). For Hydra, you push the *settings* screen from the main screen and the user goes *back*, basic stack navigation.
- **Navigation is itself a mobile-native experience:** mobile navigation (push/back transitions, tabs, the back gesture) is part of what makes an app *feel native* (the platform's navigation patterns and animations), so using the navigation library (which provides native-feeling transitions) is part of building a *native-feeling* app. Navigation isn't just routing; it's a core part of the mobile UX.
So *navigation* (via React Navigation/Expo Router) is how mobile apps are *structured into screens* and the user *moves* between them, with the *stack* (push/back) pattern as the basic one (used for Hydra's main -> settings), and it's a *fundamental*, *native-feeling* part of mobile apps. Adding the settings screen introduces this essential navigation concept.

## Forms and inputs on mobile, plus the settings pattern
Building the settings screen also involves *mobile forms/inputs* (a toggle, a time picker), previewing the deeper forms work (W5) and teaching the *settings* pattern. Mobile inputs differ from web, you use native input components (`<Switch>` for the toggle, a time picker component for the time), which provide *native* controls (a native switch, a native time-picker wheel/dialog) that *feel* native and are *touch-optimized*. The *settings* pattern, a screen where users *configure* preferences that *persist* (AsyncStorage) and *affect* the app's behavior (here, the reminder schedule), is common and teaches *connecting UI -> state -> persistence -> effect* (the toggle/picker update state, persist it, and reschedule the notification). For Hydra, the settings screen lets the user *control* their reminder (a core respect-the-user point, they choose if/when to be reminded), with native inputs (switch, time picker), persisted preferences, and the effect of rescheduling the notification. This connects several concepts, navigation (to the settings screen), native inputs (switch, time picker), state/persistence (the preferences), and effect (rescheduling), into a real, useful feature. The takeaway is that *navigation* (screens and moving between them) and *native inputs* (touch-optimized controls) are core mobile building blocks, and the *settings* pattern (configurable, persisted, effective preferences) is a common, useful one, all of which you practice building Hydra's settings screen, making the reminder properly user-controlled. (Forms/inputs/keyboard get deep treatment in W5; here you get a first, practical taste.)

## Where this fits
You built Hydra's settings screen, introducing *navigation* (React Navigation's stack push/back, how mobile apps structure and move between screens, a native-feeling core pattern) and *native inputs* (a `<Switch>`, a time picker), with the *settings* pattern (configurable, persisted preferences that affect behavior, rescheduling the reminder), making the reminder user-controlled and respectful. Tomorrow you test the reminder works.

items.title: Test the reminder
items.body:
## Testing the reminder works
Before shipping v0.2, you *test* that the reminder notification *actually works*, scheduling it, and verifying the OS delivers it at the right time, including when the app is closed. Testing notifications has some specifics:
```text
test:  - schedule a reminder (e.g. for 1-2 minutes from now, to test quickly)
       - CLOSE the app
       - confirm the notification arrives (from the OS, app closed)
       - tap it - confirm it opens the app appropriately
       - test: permission denied case, changing the time (reschedules correctly), toggle off (cancels)
```
You verify the *real* behavior, the notification *fires* (delivered by the OS), at the *right time*, *even when the app is closed* (the key property), and the surrounding cases (permission denied handled, time change reschedules, disabling cancels). Testing notifications often means scheduling one for *soon* (a minute out) to verify quickly, and *closing the app* to confirm the OS delivers it independently.

## Why testing notifications (and real-device testing) matters
Understanding *why* this testing is essential reinforces the verify-the-real-behavior discipline, with mobile specifics:
- **Notifications must be verified on a real device, in real conditions:** notification behavior (permissions, OS delivery, app-closed delivery, tapping to open) is *device-and-OS-specific* and involves the *OS* (not just your code), so you *must* test it on a *real device* (or proper simulator) in *real conditions* (app closed, real timing) to confirm it *actually* works. You can't just assume the code is right, the *real* delivery (by the OS, when the app's closed, at the right time) is what matters, and only real testing confirms it. This is the verify-the-real-behavior discipline (pervasive in the track), with the mobile specific that notifications involve OS behavior you must test on-device.
- **The "app closed" case is critical and easy to get wrong:** the *whole point* of a reminder is that it fires *when the user isn't in the app* (it brings them back), so you *must* test the *app-closed* delivery (the case that matters most and is easy to overlook, you might test with the app *open* and miss that the closed-app case has an issue). Testing with the app *closed* verifies the *real* use case. This is a mobile-specific testing consideration, test the background/closed-app behavior, not just the foreground.
- **Mobile requires real-device testing generally:** more broadly, mobile features (notifications, and later camera, location, etc.) often behave differently or only fully work on *real devices* (vs simulators), and involve *device/OS* specifics (permissions, hardware, OS delivery), so *real-device testing* is *essential* in mobile development, you test on *actual phones* (iOS *and* Android, since they differ) to verify features *really* work in *real* conditions. This is a key mobile discipline, develop with Expo Go on your phone (W1), and *test* features on real devices, because mobile behavior is device/OS-dependent and the real conditions (permissions, app state, hardware, platform differences) only show up on real devices.
So testing the reminder, on a *real device*, in *real conditions* (especially *app closed*), verifying *actual* OS delivery and the surrounding cases (permission denied, time change, toggle off), matters because notification behavior is OS/device-specific and the closed-app case is critical, embodying the verify-the-real-behavior discipline with the mobile specific of *real-device testing*.

## The discipline: real-device testing for mobile
The broader takeaway is that *real-device testing is essential in mobile development*, because mobile features depend on the *device and OS* (permissions, hardware, OS behaviors, platform differences) in ways that only fully manifest on real devices, so you *verify on real phones* (both platforms) rather than assuming code correctness or relying solely on simulators. This is the mobile version of the "verify the real behavior, don't assume" discipline (recurring across the tracks), elevated because mobile has *more* device/OS-dependent behavior (notifications, hardware, permissions, iOS-vs-Android differences) that you *must* test in *real* conditions. For Hydra's reminder, real-device testing confirms the OS *actually* delivers the daily notification when the app's closed (the real use case), which you *can't* verify any other way. And as you add more native features (camera, location, push, W9-12), real-device testing becomes *even more* essential (those features deeply involve device hardware/OS). So you build the habit *now*: *test mobile features on real devices, in real conditions, including the background/closed-app cases and on both platforms*, because that's the only way to know they *really* work. Testing Hydra's reminder this way (real device, app closed, real timing, both platforms ideally) verifies the feature genuinely works and establishes the real-device-testing discipline essential to mobile development. A notification that "should work" per the code but fails on a real closed-app device is exactly the kind of bug real-device testing catches, and shipping without it means users get a broken reminder.

## Where this fits
You tested Hydra's reminder on a real device in real conditions (especially *app closed*, the critical case), verifying actual OS delivery and the surrounding cases (permission denied, time change, toggle off), embodying the essential mobile discipline of *real-device testing* (because mobile behavior is device/OS-dependent and only fully shows up on real phones, both platforms). Tomorrow you tag v0.2 and build a new APK.

You ship Hydra v0.2, now a real daily-use app with a daily reset and reminders, versioning it and building a new APK:
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Hydra v0.2: daily reset + reminder notifications (local, OS-scheduled)"
git tag v0.2
git push
eas build --platform android --profile preview    # new APK with v0.2
```
Hydra v0.2 *resets daily* (fresh each day, via the store-date-compare-on-open pattern) and *reminds you* (a user-configured, OS-delivered daily local notification), with a *settings screen* (navigation, native inputs) to control the reminder. It's now a *genuine daily-use app*, it prompts you to hydrate daily and tracks each day fresh, which is what makes a habit tracker actually *work* (it brings you back daily). You install the new APK and *use it* (the real test, does it remind you and reset correctly day to day?).

## What v0.2 taught: fundamentally-mobile capabilities
Step back: v0.2 added the *fundamentally-mobile* capabilities that distinguish a mobile app from a web app, and that make Hydra a real daily-use product. You learned *local notifications* (scheduled by your app, *delivered by the OS even when the app's closed*, no server needed, the OS working for you, a power web lacks), the *permission model* (the OS gates capabilities behind *user consent*, so you request, handle grant/denial gracefully, respect the user, ask contextually, mobile's privacy-and-control framework), the robust *time-based-state pattern* (store timestamps, compare on access, for an intermittently-running app, vs unreliably running code at a time), *navigation* (how mobile apps structure into screens and move between them, native-feeling), *native inputs* (touch-optimized controls), and the essential *real-device testing* discipline (verify mobile features in real conditions, especially app-closed, on real phones). These, especially the OS-delivered notifications and the permission model, are *core to what makes mobile distinct and powerful* (the OS provides capabilities, gated by user consent, that work even when your app isn't running), and they make Hydra a *real* habit app (it reliably reminds you daily). v0.2 is the week mobile's *native platform powers* (and their consent model) start making Hydra genuinely useful.

## Where this fits
You shipped Hydra v0.2 with a daily reset and OS-delivered reminder notifications, a genuine daily-use habit app, having learned the fundamentally-mobile capabilities (local notifications, the permission model, time-based-state patterns, navigation, real-device testing) that distinguish mobile from web. weeks.title: Hydra v0.3: History + streaks
weeks.context:
Hydra v0.3 adds habit history (track which habits were completed on which days) and streaks (consecutive days all habits were completed). These features introduce a real data model: instead of just storing whether today's habits are checked, you store a completion record for every day. This is the point where "simple state" becomes "structured local data", and where you feel the limits of AsyncStorage.

AsyncStorage is a key-value store. It is good for simple settings (reminder time, user preferences). It becomes awkward for structured data that you want to query. To get all habits completed in the last 30 days, you either store the entire history as one JSON blob (fine until it gets large) or store keys like habit:1:2026-05-01:completed (hard to query).

For structured local data, SQLite is the right tool. expo-sqlite provides a SQLite database on device. You create tables, insert rows, and query with SQL. It is fast, supports transactions, and handles large datasets without loading everything into memory. The tradeoff: SQL schema design and migration management, which is more complex than AsyncStorage.

Streaks require date arithmetic. A streak is the number of consecutive days (ending today or yesterday) on which all habits were completed. You must define "completed day" clearly: does the day end at midnight? What if the user is still using the app at 11:59pm, does checking a habit at 11:58 count for today? For Hydra, define completion at 11:59:59pm device local time.

React Navigation and complex navigation state: Hydra v0.3 has multiple screens, HabitList (today), History (calendar view), and Settings. You add a tab navigator with three tabs. Tab bars are a core mobile navigation pattern, the bottom tab bar is how most mobile apps switch between primary sections of the app.

items.title: Plan the history view
items.body:
## Real data: history and streaks
Hydra v0.3 adds **habit history** (track which habits were completed on which days) and **streaks** (consecutive days of completion), features that require a *real data model*. Until now, you stored just *today's* state (is today done?); history requires storing a *completion record for every day*, structured data over time. This is the point where **"simple state" becomes "structured local data"**, and where you *feel the limits of AsyncStorage*. So this week is about graduating from simple key-value persistence to a *real local database*, and building the history/streaks features that turn Hydra into a tracker with *memory* and *motivation* (streaks).

## When AsyncStorage isn't enough
The pivotal realization is *why AsyncStorage becomes awkward* for this, which teaches the mobile-storage progression:
- **AsyncStorage is a key-value store, good for simple data:** AsyncStorage (W1) is *good* for *simple* settings (the reminder time, preferences), small key-value data. It's the right tool for *simple* persistence. But...
- **It becomes awkward for structured data you want to *query*:** history is *structured* (a record per day, per habit) that you want to *query* ("all habits completed in the last 30 days," "the current streak"). With AsyncStorage, you'd either *store the entire history as one JSON blob* (fine until it gets *large*, then loading/saving the whole blob every change is slow and clumsy) or *store keys like `habit:1:2026-05-01:completed`* (hard to *query*, you can't easily ask "the last 30 days" across such keys). Both are *awkward*, AsyncStorage *isn't built* for structured, queryable data, so using it for history is fighting the tool. This is *feeling the limits of AsyncStorage*, it's great for simple key-value, awkward for structured/queryable data.
- **For structured local data, SQLite is the right tool:** when you need *structured*, *queryable* local data (like history), the right tool is **SQLite**, a *real relational database* on the device. `expo-sqlite` provides a SQLite database in your app, so you can store *structured* data (tables, rows) and *query* it (SQL), which is exactly what history/streaks need ("get completions for the last 30 days," "compute the streak"). SQLite is the *right* tool for structured local data, just as Postgres was for the backend (W10 of full-stack), and you reach for it when AsyncStorage's key-value model becomes awkward.
So the realization is: *AsyncStorage for simple key-value data, SQLite for structured/queryable data*, and history/streaks (structured, queryable) is where you *graduate* to SQLite, feeling AsyncStorage's limits and reaching for the right tool. (There's also MMKV for fast key-value, W8; the point is matching the storage tool to the data, the mobile version of the web track's storage-categorization.)

## Where this fits
This week grows Hydra to v0.3 with *history* and *streaks*, requiring a *real data model* (a completion record per day), where you graduate from AsyncStorage (simple key-value) to *SQLite* (structured, queryable local data) and build features that give Hydra memory and motivation. Today's orientation: history/streaks need *structured, queryable* local data, AsyncStorage (key-value) becomes *awkward* for this, so you reach for *SQLite* (a real local relational database, the right tool for structured data), the mobile version of matching the storage tool to the data. Tomorrow you plan the history view and design the data.

items.title: Compute streaks
items.body:
## Computing streaks from history
You add **streaks**, the count of *consecutive days* all habits were completed, a motivating feature computed *from* the history data. Streaks require *logic over the historical data*:
```jsx
function computeStreak(completionsByDate) {
  let streak = 0;
  let day = today();
  while (allHabitsCompletedOn(day, completionsByDate)) {   // walk backward from today
    streak++;
    day = previousDay(day);                                 // ...while each prior day is complete
  }
  return streak;                                            // consecutive complete days
}
```
You *query* the completion history (SQLite) and *compute* the streak, count consecutive days (backward from today) where all habits were completed, stopping at the first incomplete day. This turns the raw history into a *motivating metric* (the current streak), which is psychologically powerful for habit-building (people want to *maintain* their streak).

## Why streaks: logic over data, and motivation
Understanding streaks teaches *computing derived values from data* and the *product value* of such metrics:
- **Streaks are a *derived* value, computed from the data:** the streak isn't *stored* directly; it's *computed* from the completion history (consecutive complete days). This is *deriving* a meaningful value *from* your data (the data-logic-output pattern), you have the *raw* data (completions per day) and *compute* a *derived insight* (the streak) from it. This *computing derived values from stored data* is a common, important pattern (streaks, stats, summaries, aggregates), and it's why you stored *structured* history (SQLite): so you *can* query and compute over it. Streaks demonstrate the *payoff* of the structured data model, you can now *compute* meaningful insights from the history.
- **The logic must be correct (edge cases):** computing streaks *correctly* involves *edge cases*, what counts as "today" (timezones, the daily-reset boundary), gaps (a missed day breaks the streak), partial completion (all habits vs some), and getting these right requires care (the guard-the-edge-cases discipline). So streak logic is a place to think carefully about *correctness* (define "consecutive complete days" precisely, handle the boundaries). Computing derived values *correctly* (handling edge cases) is part of the skill.
- **Streaks are motivating (product value):** beyond the technical, streaks are *powerful product features*, they *motivate* users (the desire to *maintain* a streak drives daily engagement, exactly what a habit tracker wants). This is *product thinking*, a *derived metric* (streak) that *motivates* the user, turning data into *engagement*. So streaks aren't just a calculation; they're a *motivational feature* that makes Hydra *stickier* (users return to keep their streak). Recognizing the *product value* of such metrics (turning tracked data into motivating feedback) is valuable product insight.
So streaks teach *computing derived values from your data* (the streak from the history, the payoff of structured storage), doing it *correctly* (edge cases), and the *product value* of such metrics (streaks motivate engagement, turning data into stickiness). Hydra's streak feature is both a technical exercise (logic over data) and a product one (a motivating metric).

## Why this matters: data enables insight and engagement
The deeper point is that *structured data enables computing insights/metrics that add real value*, and Hydra's streaks exemplify the *progression* from *storing* data to *deriving value* from it. By storing *structured* history (SQLite, W3-D2), you *enabled* computing *derived insights* (streaks, and stats, D5) that you *couldn't* easily get from simple state, the structured data *unlocks* the insights. This is a general, important pattern: *store data well (structured), and you can compute valuable insights from it* (streaks, stats, trends, summaries), which often *are* the app's value (a tracker's value is largely the *insights* it gives you about your tracked behavior, your history, streaks, stats). So the progression, *track* data (store it structured) -> *compute insights* (streaks, stats) -> *deliver value/engagement* (the user sees their progress, is motivated), is the core of what makes a *tracking* app valuable, and Hydra's streaks are a key example (the streak is a *motivating insight* derived from the *structured history*). For mobile (and apps generally), this means *think about the insights/value you can derive from data*, not just storing it, the *derived metrics* (streaks, stats) are often where the user value is. Hydra v0.3's streaks turn the raw history into a *motivating, valuable* feature, demonstrating that *structured data + derived insights = real product value*. Computing streaks well (correct logic, from the structured data, delivering motivation) shows the full arc from data to value, which is what makes Hydra a genuinely useful and engaging tracker.

## Where this fits
You compute Hydra's streaks: a *derived* value (consecutive complete days) computed *from* the structured history, requiring correct logic (edge cases), and delivering *product value* (streaks motivate engagement). This demonstrates the progression from *storing* structured data to *deriving valuable insights* from it (the payoff of the SQLite data model), turning tracked data into motivating feedback. Tomorrow you build a stats screen with more derived insights.
