items.title: Streak calc
Stats screen
items.body:
## Stats screen: more insights from the data
You build a **Stats screen** showing *more insights* derived from Hydra's history, completion rates, trends, totals, weekly/monthly summaries, giving the user a richer view of their tracked behavior:
```text
stats screen:  - overall completion rate (% of habits completed)
               - this week vs last week
               - best streak, current streak
               - a simple chart (completions over time)
               - per-habit stats (which habits you keep, which you miss)
```
You *query* the history (SQLite) and *compute/aggregate* various stats (rates, trends, totals, bests), displaying them (numbers, maybe a simple chart). The Stats screen *deepens* Hydra's value, beyond the streak, it gives the user *insight* into their behavior (how often, trends, which habits stick), which is much of *why* people use a tracker (to *understand* their behavior). More derived insights = more value.

## Computing and presenting insights
Building the Stats screen teaches *aggregating data into insights* and *presenting them clearly*:
- **Aggregate the data into meaningful metrics:** stats are *aggregations/computations* over the history, completion *rates* (completed/total), *trends* (this week vs last), *totals*, *bests* (longest streak), *per-category* breakdowns (per habit). You *query* the structured history and *compute* these aggregates (with SQL aggregation and/or JS logic), turning raw records into *meaningful metrics*. This is *data aggregation/analysis* (the same kind of thinking as the data-analysis track, applied to your app's data), computing insightful summaries from the raw data. Choosing *which* metrics are *meaningful* (the ones that give the user useful insight, completion rate, trends, streaks) is part of the skill, you compute the stats that *matter* to the user, not arbitrary numbers.
- **Present insights clearly (visualization):** stats must be *presented clearly* so the user *understands* them, clear numbers with context (labels, comparisons), and *simple visualizations* (a chart of completions over time, a progress ring) where a *visual* conveys the insight better than a number. *Presenting* data well (clear, labeled, visualized appropriately) is part of making stats *valuable*, a confusing stats screen (raw numbers, no context) doesn't help; a clear one (labeled metrics, a simple trend chart) gives *insight*. So you present stats *clearly* (good labels, context, simple charts), making the insights *accessible*. (Mobile charting libraries, or simple custom visuals, render the charts.)
- **It's the data-to-insight-to-presentation pipeline:** the Stats screen is the full *data -> insight -> presentation* pipeline, *query* the structured data, *compute* meaningful aggregates, *present* them clearly (numbers + visuals), which is the core of turning tracked data into user value. This pipeline (store structured -> aggregate into insights -> present clearly) is how *any* data-driven insight feature works.
So the Stats screen teaches *aggregating data into meaningful metrics* (rates, trends, bests, the data-analysis thinking) and *presenting them clearly* (labeled numbers, simple charts), the *data -> insight -> presentation* pipeline that delivers the *insight* value of a tracking app.

## Why insights are the value of a tracker
The deeper point, building on streaks (D4), is that *the insights derived from tracked data are largely the value of a tracking app*, so building good *stats/insights* (well-computed, clearly presented) is building the *core value*. People track things (habits, hydration, anything) ultimately to *understand* and *improve* their behavior, and the *insights* (am I doing well? trending up? which habits stick? what's my streak?) are *what they want* from the tracking. So a tracker's value is largely its *insights*, the raw tracking is the *input*, the *insights* (stats, streaks, trends) are the *output the user cares about*. This means building *good* insight features, computing *meaningful* metrics (the ones that give real understanding) and *presenting* them *clearly* (so the user *gets* the insight), is building the *heart* of the app's value. For Hydra, the stats and streaks are *why* tracking hydration is *useful* (they show you your patterns, motivate you, help you improve), without them, you're just checking boxes; *with* them, you *understand* and *improve* your hydration. So Hydra v0.3's stats screen, deriving and presenting insights from the structured history, delivers the *core value* of a tracker. The broader takeaway for mobile (and apps) is that, for any app that *tracks* or *collects* data, *the insights you derive and present are often the real value*, so you invest in *good* insight features (meaningful metrics, clear presentation), which is the *data -> insight -> value* arc that turns *collecting* data into *helping* the user. Hydra's stats (and streaks) embody this, structured data, well-aggregated into meaningful insights, clearly presented, delivering the understanding-and-motivation that makes a tracker valuable. Building insight features well is building the product's heart.

## Where this fits
You built Hydra's Stats screen, *aggregating* the structured history into *meaningful insights* (rates, trends, streaks, the data-analysis thinking) and *presenting* them clearly (labeled metrics, simple charts), the *data -> insight -> presentation* pipeline that delivers the *insight* value (understanding and motivation) that is largely the *point* of a tracking app. Tomorrow you polish v0.3 with animations.

items.title: Polish + animations
items.body:
## Polish v0.3 with animations
You polish Hydra v0.3 with **animations**, smooth, delightful motion that makes the app feel *native* and *alive*, a fill animation as a glass fills, a satisfying streak celebration, smooth screen transitions, animated stat reveals. Mobile users *expect* fluid animation (it's a hallmark of quality native apps):
```text
- the glass smoothly FILLS when tapped (not an instant jump)
- a celebration animation when you complete all habits / extend a streak
- smooth transitions between screens, animated chart/stat reveals
- micro-interactions: things respond fluidly to touch
```
You add *tasteful*, *smooth* animations (using React Native's Animated API, or better, **Reanimated**, the standard for performant mobile animation) that make interactions feel *fluid* and *delightful*, the glass filling smoothly, a streak celebration, polished transitions, which significantly elevates how the app *feels*. (Animations get deep treatment in W6; here you add foundational polish animations to v0.3.)

## Why animation matters on mobile (and doing it performantly)
Understanding *why* animation is so important on mobile, and the performance angle, frames it:
- **Smooth animation is a hallmark of native quality (high mobile expectations):** mobile users are accustomed to *highly polished*, *fluidly animated* native apps (the platform's apps, top App Store apps), so smooth animation is *expected*, and its *absence* (janky or no animation, instant jarring changes) makes an app feel *cheap/non-native*. *Fluid* animation (smooth transitions, responsive micro-interactions, satisfying feedback) is much of what makes an app feel *native, polished, and delightful*. So animation isn't just decoration; it's a *core* part of meeting mobile's *high quality bar* and feeling *native*. (This is the W6 theme, "where mobile feels native", previewed.)
- **Performance is critical, animations must run at 60fps (use the right tools):** the *catch* is that animation must be *smooth* (60fps, no jank/stutter), and *janky* animation (dropped frames) is *worse* than none (it feels broken). Achieving smooth animation on mobile requires the *right approach*, animations that run on the *native* thread / UI thread (not blocked by JavaScript), which is why **Reanimated** (which runs animations natively, off the JS thread) is the standard for *performant* mobile animation (vs the basic Animated API, which can jank if the JS thread is busy). So you do animation *performantly* (Reanimated, native-driven animations) to ensure *smooth* 60fps motion. *Performant* animation is the goal, smooth, not janky, which requires the right tools/approach. (This connects to mobile performance, W17, animations are a key place performance matters.)
- **Tasteful, purposeful animation (restraint, again):** as on web (W2/W6 of full-stack), animation should be *tasteful and purposeful* (smooth feedback, satisfying micro-interactions, guiding transitions), *not* excessive (overdone animation is distracting and can hurt performance). So you animate *purposefully* (the glass fill, the celebration, smooth transitions) and *tastefully* (enhancing, not overwhelming), the restraint discipline. And *accessibly*, respecting reduced-motion preferences (the accessibility theme, mobile users can request reduced motion too).
So animation matters on mobile because *smooth animation is a hallmark of native quality* (expected, and its absence feels cheap), it must be done *performantly* (60fps, via Reanimated/native-driven animation, since jank is worse than none), and *tastefully* (purposeful, restrained, accessible). Adding good animations to Hydra v0.3 elevates its *feel* toward native polish.

## Why this matters: feel is a feature on mobile
The deeper point is that, *on mobile especially, how an app *feels* (its fluidity, responsiveness, animation, polish) is a *feature*, often as important as what it does*, because mobile's quality bar is high and users *judge* and *enjoy* apps largely through their *feel*. A mobile app that *does* the right things but *feels* janky, unresponsive, or unpolished is experienced as *low quality* (and users have polished alternatives), while one that *feels* fluid, responsive, and delightful (smooth animations, satisfying interactions) is experienced as *high quality* (and is more *enjoyable* to use, driving engagement/retention). So *feel*, the fluid animations, the responsive micro-interactions, the polish, is a *core part of mobile app quality*, not a nicety, it's much of what *distinguishes* a great mobile app, and it directly affects how users *perceive*, *enjoy*, and *stick with* the app. This is the *polish/perceived-quality* theme (web W23) *intensified* on mobile (where the bar is higher and *feel* is so central to the experience). For Hydra, adding smooth animations (the satisfying glass fill, the streak celebration, fluid transitions) makes it *feel* like a *real, polished, delightful* app, which is much of what makes it *enjoyable* to use daily (and thus *effective* as a habit tracker, you *want* to open it). The takeaway is that *on mobile, invest in feel*, smooth, performant, tasteful animation and responsive polish, because *feel is a feature* that significantly determines perceived quality and enjoyment, and it's central to what makes a mobile app *great* (not just functional). Hydra v0.3's animation polish moves it toward that native-quality feel, and W6 will deepen this "where mobile feels native" focus. Animation and fluid feel are core mobile quality, and you start building them into Hydra now.

## Where this fits
You polished Hydra v0.3 with *tasteful, performant animations* (smooth glass fill, streak celebration, fluid transitions, via Reanimated for native-driven 60fps motion), because *smooth animation is a hallmark of native quality* (expected on mobile, janky is worse than none), and *feel is a feature* on mobile (fluidity and polish are core to perceived quality and enjoyment, intensified vs web). Tomorrow you tag and ship v0.3.

You ship Hydra v0.3, now a tracker with memory, insight, and polish:

weeks.title: Hydra v0.4: TypeScript + cleanup
weeks.context:
Hydra v0.4 refactors the entire codebase to TypeScript and introduces the architectural patterns that make mobile apps maintainable as they grow. Up to this point, you have been building features quickly; now you pay off the technical debt by typing everything and organising the code properly.

TypeScript on React Native is the same TypeScript you have seen before with a few mobile-specific types. The React Native type definitions come from @types/react-native (or are bundled with the library). Expo SDKs are typed. The types you will add this week: explicit prop types for every component, typed navigation params (what data is passed between screens), typed database query results, typed AsyncStorage values.

Typed navigation is one of the most valuable additions to a React Native + TypeScript codebase. React Navigation provides a way to define the type of parameters each screen accepts: type RootStackParamList = { HabitDetail: { habitId: number }; Settings: undefined }. Once you define this, the navigate function is type-checked, you cannot navigate to HabitDetail without providing a habitId. And in HabitDetail, useRoute<RouteProp<RootStackParamList, 'HabitDetail'>>() gives you typed params.

Code organisation: by W4, Hydra has enough screens and logic that a flat file structure becomes hard to navigate. Standard React Native project structure: /screens (one file per screen), /components (reusable components), /hooks (custom React hooks for shared logic), /services (database, notifications, AsyncStorage abstractions), /utils (pure functions: date formatting, streak calculation), /types (shared TypeScript interfaces and types). Move code into this structure this week.

Custom hooks encapsulate stateful logic. The useHabits hook manages the habits list state and provides functions (addHabit, toggleHabit, deleteHabit). The useStreak hook queries the database and returns the current streak. Components just call these hooks and render, they contain no business logic.

items.title: Why TypeScript
items.body:
## Paying off the debt: TypeScript and structure
Hydra v0.4 **refactors the entire codebase to TypeScript** and introduces the **architectural patterns** that keep mobile apps maintainable as they grow. Up to now, you've built features *quickly* (accumulating some technical debt); now you *pay it off* by *typing everything* and *organizing the code properly*. This is the engineering-maturity week, taking a working-but-quickly-built app and making it *solid*, *typed*, and *well-structured* so it stays maintainable as it grows (toward the real, complex app the rest of the track builds). It's the same "refactor to quality" step you saw in other tracks (FlightWise's tuning, Bean Forge's Astro refactor), here: TypeScript + architecture for a mobile app.

## Why TypeScript: catching errors before they ship
**TypeScript** adds *static types* to JavaScript, catching a whole class of errors *at compile time* (in your editor) rather than at *runtime* (on the user's phone), which matters even more on mobile:
```text
JavaScript:   errors (wrong type, typo, missing field) surface at RUNTIME - on the user's device
TypeScript:   the compiler catches them at DEVELOPMENT time - in your editor, before shipping
```
The case for TypeScript (which you may know from web) is *especially* compelling on mobile:
- **Mobile bugs reach users harder-to-fix:** a runtime bug in a *deployed mobile app* is *worse* than on web, you can't just push a fix instantly (app updates go through stores/review, W22, and users must update), so a bug that *ships* lingers. So *catching* bugs *before* shipping (TypeScript) is *especially* valuable on mobile, where shipped bugs are costlier to fix. TypeScript's compile-time error-catching directly reduces the bugs that *reach* users' devices.
- **It makes refactoring and growth safe:** as the codebase *grows* (Hydra toward a real app), TypeScript's types make *changing* code *safe*, the compiler catches what your change breaks (a renamed field, a changed function signature), so you can refactor and add features *confidently* (the same "types enable fearless change" benefit as tests). For a *growing* app, this is essential maintainability. TypeScript is the foundation for *safely* growing the codebase.
- **It's documentation and autocomplete:** types *document* the code (what shape is this data? what does this function take?) and power *autocomplete* (the editor knows the types, guiding you), making the code *easier to work with* and *understand*, valuable as the app and (eventually) team grow.
So TypeScript catches errors at *development* time (not on users' devices), which is *especially* valuable on mobile (shipped bugs are costly to fix), makes *refactoring/growth safe*, and serves as *documentation/autocomplete*, all the engineering-maturity benefits that make a *growing* mobile app *maintainable* and *reliable*.

## Where this fits
This week refactors Hydra to v0.4: *TypeScript* (typed everything, catching errors before they ship) and *architectural patterns* (organizing the code for maintainability), the engineering-maturity step that makes the codebase *solid* for future growth. It completes the Foundations phase. Today's orientation: you *pay off technical debt* by adding TypeScript (which catches errors at development time, *especially* valuable on mobile where shipped bugs are costly to fix, and makes growth/refactoring safe) and proper architecture, making Hydra maintainable as it grows. Tomorrow you start the migration (App.js to App.tsx).

items.title: Migrate App.js to App.tsx
items.body:
## Migrating to TypeScript, and typing on React Native
You migrate Hydra to TypeScript, starting with the entry point (App.js -> App.tsx) and working through the code, adding types. TypeScript on React Native is *the same TypeScript* you may know, with a few *mobile-specific* types:
```tsx
// component props, typed:
type GlassProps = { filled: boolean; onPress: () => void };
function Glass({ filled, onPress }: GlassProps) { ... }
// typed state, typed function signatures, etc.
```
The migration is *incremental*, rename `.js` to `.tsx` (for components) / `.ts`, add types gradually (TypeScript allows gradual typing, you can migrate piece by piece), and fix the type errors that surface (which often *reveal* real bugs, mismatched types you didn't notice). The React Native type definitions come from `@types/react-native` (or are bundled), and Expo SDKs are *typed*, so you get types for RN and Expo APIs. You add: *explicit prop types* for every component, *typed state*, *typed function signatures*, gradually making the whole codebase typed.

## What to type, and the mobile-specific types
Understanding *what* to type (and the RN-specific types) makes the migration effective:
- **Component props (the most important):** typing *every component's props* (what data each component takes) is the *highest-value* typing, it documents and enforces each component's interface, catching wrong/missing props at compile time. So you add *explicit prop types* (a `type`/`interface` for each component's props), the foundational TypeScript-on-React-discipline. Typed props make components *self-documenting* and *safe to use* (the compiler checks you pass the right props).
- **React Native and Expo APIs are typed (you benefit):** `@types/react-native` types the RN components/APIs, and Expo SDKs are typed, so when you use RN/Expo APIs, you get *type-checking and autocomplete* (the compiler knows `<FlatList>`'s props, `Notifications.scheduleNotificationAsync`'s signature, etc.). So you *benefit* from the platform's types (catching misuse, guiding usage), part of why typing RN code is smooth (the libraries are typed). You type *your* code (props, state, data) and *consume* the platform's types.
- **Typed data (SQLite results, AsyncStorage values, state):** you type your *data*, the shape of SQLite query results (a `Completion` type), AsyncStorage values, your state, so data flows through the app *typed* (you know the shape of the data everywhere). This catches data-shape mismatches (using a field that doesn't exist, wrong types) at compile time, valuable given how much of an app is *data flow*. So typing the *data* (results, stored values, state) is key.
So you migrate *incrementally* (rename, type gradually, fix errors), typing *component props* (highest value, self-documenting interfaces), *benefiting* from RN/Expo's types (type-checking/autocomplete on platform APIs), and typing your *data* (SQLite results, stored values, state), making the codebase progressively typed and safer.

## Why the migration reveals (and prevents) bugs
The deeper value, beyond future safety, is that *the act of adding types often reveals existing bugs and prevents future ones*, which is why the migration is worth doing carefully. As you add types, the compiler *flags* places where types *don't match*, and these mismatches are *often real bugs* you hadn't noticed (a function called with the wrong type, a field accessed that might be undefined, a data shape that doesn't match its usage), so the migration *surfaces latent bugs* (the "fix the type errors and you fix real bugs" experience). So adding TypeScript isn't just *future* safety; it *immediately* finds *existing* problems (the type errors reveal real mismatches). And going forward, the types *prevent* whole classes of bugs (wrong types, typos, undefined access, mismatched data) from *ever* being written (the compiler catches them as you code). For a mobile app especially (where shipped bugs are costly, W4-D1), this *bug-prevention* (and *bug-revealing*) value is significant, the types are a *safety net* that catches errors *before they reach users' devices*. So the migration *pays off* immediately (revealing latent bugs as you fix type errors) and ongoing (preventing future bugs via compile-time checking), which is exactly the "pay off technical debt" the week is about, you're investing in a *typed, safer* codebase that has *fewer* bugs *now* (the ones the migration reveals) and *will* have fewer *future* bugs (the ones types prevent). This makes Hydra more *reliable* (fewer bugs reaching users) and more *maintainable* (safe to change), the engineering-maturity payoff. Doing the migration thoroughly (typing props, data, fixing the revealed errors) is worth it because it *finds* and *prevents* real bugs, directly improving the app's reliability.

## Where this fits
You migrate Hydra to TypeScript incrementally (rename, type gradually, fix errors), typing *component props* (highest value), benefiting from RN/Expo's typed APIs, and typing your *data* (SQLite results, stored values, state), which *reveals latent bugs* (as you fix type errors) and *prevents future ones* (compile-time checking), especially valuable on mobile where shipped bugs are costly. Tomorrow you continue migrating components, and meet a key mobile typing win: typed navigation.

items.title: Rename + type
Migrate components
items.body:
## Typed navigation: a major mobile TypeScript win
As you migrate the components, you add **typed navigation**, which the context calls *one of the most valuable additions to a React Native + TypeScript codebase*. Navigation passes *data between screens* (navigate to a detail screen *with* an item's id), and *typing* that data flow is hugely valuable:
```tsx
// define the screens and their params (the data each screen receives):
type RootStackParamList = {
  Home: undefined;                        // Home takes no params
  HabitDetail: { habitId: number };       // HabitDetail requires a habitId
  Settings: undefined;
};
// now navigation is TYPE-CHECKED:
navigation.navigate('HabitDetail', { habitId: 5 });   // ✓ - correct params
navigation.navigate('HabitDetail', { id: 5 });        // ✗ compile error - wrong param!
```
You *define* the navigation structure with *typed params* (what data each screen receives), and then React Navigation *type-checks* your navigation, you *can't* navigate to a screen with the *wrong* params (missing, misnamed, wrong type), the compiler catches it. This makes *passing data between screens* (a common source of bugs) *type-safe*.

## Why typed navigation is so valuable
Understanding *why* typed navigation is such a win shows the value of typing the *data flow* through your app:
- **Navigation is a key data-flow boundary, and a common bug source:** moving between screens *with data* (navigate to detail *with* an id, to edit *with* an item) is a *core* mobile pattern *and* a *common source of bugs*, passing the *wrong* data (misnamed param, wrong type, forgotten param) to a screen, which then *breaks* (the screen expects `habitId` but got `id`). Without types, these bugs surface at *runtime* (the screen crashes or misbehaves); *with* typed navigation, they're caught at *compile time* (you *can't* navigate with wrong params). So typed navigation *eliminates* a whole class of common, annoying screen-to-screen data bugs. Since navigation/screen-data is so central to mobile apps, this is *high-value* typing.
- **It documents the screen interfaces:** the typed param list *documents* what data each screen *needs* (Home: nothing; HabitDetail: a habitId), so the navigation structure is *self-documenting* (you can *see* what each screen expects), which aids understanding and correct usage. The types make the app's *screen-data contracts* explicit.
- **It makes refactoring screens/navigation safe:** if you *change* a screen's params (it now needs an extra field, or a different type), the compiler flags *every* navigation call that's now wrong, so you can *safely* refactor the navigation/screen-data (the compiler ensures all the call sites are updated). For a *growing* app (more screens, more data flow), this *safe-refactoring* of navigation is very valuable.
So typed navigation is *one of the most valuable* RN+TypeScript additions because navigation/screen-data is a *central*, *bug-prone* part of mobile apps, and typing it *eliminates* common screen-to-screen data bugs (caught at compile time), *documents* the screen interfaces, and makes navigation refactoring *safe*, high-value typing for the data flow that's so central to mobile apps.

## The principle: type the boundaries and data flow
The deeper lesson is *type the boundaries and data flow of your app*, the places where data *passes between* parts (navigation between screens, props between components, data from storage/APIs), because those *boundaries* are where *type mismatches* (and thus bugs) commonly occur, and typing them *catches* those bugs. Navigation (data between screens), props (data between components), and data sources (SQLite results, AsyncStorage, later APIs) are the key *boundaries* where data *flows* through your app, and they're exactly where *wrong shapes/types* cause bugs (wrong props, wrong nav params, wrong data shape). *Typing* these boundaries (typed props, typed navigation, typed data) makes the *data flow* through the app *type-checked* end to end, so a mismatch *anywhere* (wrong prop, wrong nav param, wrong data field) is *caught at compile time*. This is the high-value typing strategy: *type the boundaries and data flow* (props, navigation, data), where the bugs are, rather than obsessing over typing trivial internals. For Hydra (and any RN app), this means: typed *props* (component boundaries), typed *navigation* (screen boundaries), typed *data* (storage/API boundaries), which together make the app's *data flow* safe, catching the common mismatch bugs before they ship. Typed navigation is the standout example (the screen-data boundary, so central to mobile), but the principle, *type the boundaries where data flows between parts*, is what makes TypeScript *high-value* in a mobile app, it catches the data-flow bugs that are common and (on mobile) costly. Applying this (typing props, navigation, and data), Hydra's data flow becomes type-safe, eliminating a major class of bugs.

## Where this fits
You add *typed navigation* (typed screen params, so navigating with wrong data is a compile error), *one of the most valuable* RN+TypeScript additions because navigation/screen-data is central and bug-prone, eliminating common screen-to-screen data bugs, documenting screen interfaces, and making navigation refactoring safe, exemplifying the principle of *typing the boundaries and data flow* (props, navigation, data) where the bugs are. Tomorrow you add tests.

## Linting and formatting: automated code quality
You add **linting** (ESLint) and **formatting** (Prettier) to Hydra, automated tools that enforce *code quality* and *consistency*:
```bash
# ESLint: catches problems and enforces best practices
# Prettier: auto-formats code to a consistent style
```
- **ESLint** *analyzes* your code for *problems* (likely bugs, bad practices, anti-patterns) and *enforces* rules (consistent practices, catching common mistakes), flagging issues as you code (and in CI). It catches a class of problems *automatically* (unused variables, likely-bug patterns, RN/React-specific gotchas).
- **Prettier** *auto-formats* your code to a *consistent* style (spacing, quotes, line breaks), so *all* the code looks *uniform* (no debates or inconsistency over formatting), applied automatically (on save, in CI). It eliminates formatting inconsistency and effort.
Together, ESLint (catch problems, enforce practices) and Prettier (consistent formatting) provide *automated code quality*, keeping the codebase *clean*, *consistent*, and *free of a class of issues*, with little manual effort.

## Why linting and formatting matter
Understanding the value of these tools shows why they're standard:
- **They catch a class of problems automatically (ESLint):** ESLint *automatically* catches *likely bugs* and *bad practices* (unused code, missing dependencies in hooks, React/RN anti-patterns, common mistakes), problems you might miss, flagged *as you code*. This is *automated* problem-catching (like TypeScript and tests, another safety layer), reducing bugs and enforcing good practices *without* manual review for these issues. ESLint is an automated quality net for a class of problems.
- **Consistent formatting aids readability and removes friction (Prettier):** *consistent* code formatting makes the codebase *easier to read* (uniform style, no jarring inconsistency) and *removes* the *friction* of formatting (no manual formatting effort, no style debates, no inconsistent code), Prettier *auto-formats* everything uniformly. This *consistency* matters more as the codebase (and team) grows (uniform code is easier to read and maintain), and it *saves* effort (automated). So Prettier gives *effortless consistency*, aiding readability and removing formatting friction.
- **They enforce quality automatically, especially valuable in a team/growing codebase:** together, these tools *automatically* enforce code quality and consistency, valuable *especially* as the codebase *grows* (and on a team), they keep the code *clean and consistent* *automatically* (in your editor and in CI), so quality doesn't degrade as the code grows. They're a low-effort, high-value part of a *maintainable* codebase (automated quality enforcement). They fit into CI (W19 of web's CI/CD applies, lint/format checks in CI) to enforce quality on every change.
So linting (ESLint, automated problem/bad-practice catching) and formatting (Prettier, effortless consistent formatting) provide *automated code quality* that catches a class of problems, ensures consistency, aids readability, and removes friction, low-effort, high-value tooling that keeps a *growing* codebase clean and quality-consistent, especially valuable as the app/team grows.

## Quality tooling as part of engineering maturity
The deeper point is that *automated quality tooling (linting, formatting, plus TypeScript and tests) is part of engineering maturity, building a codebase that stays clean and reliable as it grows*, which is the *theme* of this v0.4 week. Hydra has accumulated some technical debt (built quickly), and v0.4 *pays it off* and *builds the foundation* for *maintainable growth* via the engineering-quality tooling: *TypeScript* (type safety, catch type bugs, safe refactoring), *tests* (behavior safety, catch logic/component bugs, confident change), *linting* (catch problems/bad-practices automatically), and *formatting* (effortless consistency). *Together*, these form an *automated quality net* that keeps the codebase *clean, consistent, typed, and tested*, so it stays *maintainable and reliable* as it *grows* (toward the real, complex app the rest of the track builds). This *engineering maturity*, the quality tooling that enables *sustainable growth*, is what distinguishes a *professionally-built* app (that stays solid as it scales) from a *quickly-hacked* one (that becomes an unmaintainable mess). For a mobile app *especially* (where reliability matters and shipped bugs are costly), this quality foundation is valuable. So adding linting and formatting (alongside TypeScript and tests) completes Hydra's *engineering-maturity* upgrade: a *typed, tested, linted, formatted* codebase that's *clean, consistent, reliable, and safe to grow*. The takeaway is that *quality tooling (types, tests, lint, format) is foundational to maintainable software*, and v0.4 establishes it for Hydra, paying off the debt and building the foundation for the app to grow *without* degrading into a mess. This automated quality net is part of professional engineering, and you put it in place for Hydra now, ensuring it stays solid as it grows through the rest of the track.

You add *linting* (ESLint, automated catching of problems and bad practices) and *formatting* (Prettier, effortless consistent style), automated code-quality tooling that catches a class of problems, ensures consistency, aids readability, and removes friction, which (with TypeScript and tests) forms the *engineering-maturity* quality net that keeps a *growing* codebase clean, consistent, and reliable. items.body:
## Cleaning up: organization and a CHANGELOG
You finish the v0.4 cleanup by *organizing the code properly* and adding a **CHANGELOG**, the *architectural patterns* and *documentation* that make the app maintainable. Organization includes:
```text
- a sensible folder structure (components/, screens/, lib/, hooks/, types/ - organized by role)
- extracting reusable pieces (shared components, utility functions, custom hooks)
- separating concerns (UI components vs business logic vs data access)
- consistent patterns across the codebase
- a CHANGELOG (a record of what changed in each version: v0.1, v0.2, v0.3, v0.4...)
```
You *organize* the code into a *clean structure* (folders by role, extracted reusable pieces, separated concerns), apply *consistent patterns*, and add a *CHANGELOG* documenting the version history. This *architectural* cleanup makes the codebase *navigable*, *maintainable*, and *understandable*, paying off the "built quickly" debt with proper structure.

## Why organization and architecture matter as apps grow
Understanding *why* code organization matters (increasingly as the app grows) frames this:
- **Good structure makes a growing codebase navigable and maintainable:** as an app *grows* (more screens, components, logic, the real app Hydra becomes), a *disorganized* codebase becomes a *mess* (hard to find things, hard to change safely, tangled concerns), while a *well-organized* one (clear structure, separated concerns, reusable pieces, consistent patterns) stays *navigable* and *maintainable* (you can *find* code, *understand* it, *change* it safely). So *organization* is what keeps a *growing* codebase *workable*, the larger the app, the more the structure matters. Good architecture is the foundation for *sustainable growth*.
- **Separation of concerns and reusability:** organizing means *separating concerns* (UI components separate from business logic separate from data access, so each is focused and changeable independently) and *extracting reusable pieces* (shared components, utilities, custom hooks, so you don't duplicate, and changes are centralized), the same component/modularity discipline from across the tracks, applied to the whole app's architecture. These patterns (separation, reusability, consistency) make the code *cleaner* and *more maintainable*, each piece focused, reusable, and consistently structured. For mobile, *custom hooks* (extracting reusable stateful logic, e.g. a `useHabits` hook) are a particularly valuable pattern for organizing logic.
- **Consistency across the codebase:** *consistent* patterns (the same way of doing things throughout, file organization, naming, component structure) make the codebase *predictable* and *easy to work in* (you know where things are and how they're done), valuable as it grows (and for a team). Consistency is part of good architecture.
So code organization/architecture matters because *it keeps a growing codebase navigable, maintainable, and understandable* (vs a disorganized mess), via *separation of concerns* (focused, independently-changeable parts), *reusability* (extracted shared pieces, custom hooks), and *consistency* (predictable patterns), the architectural foundation for *sustainable growth*, increasingly important as the app grows.

## Documentation, version history, and the maturity mindset
The CHANGELOG and the broader cleanup reflect a *maturity mindset*, documenting and structuring the project for the long term, which completes the v0.4 engineering-maturity theme. A **CHANGELOG** (recording what changed in each version, v0.1 tap-to-fill, v0.2 reminders, v0.3 history/streaks, v0.4 TypeScript/cleanup) *documents the project's evolution*, useful for understanding the history, communicating changes (to users or collaborators), and the discipline of *tracking* what you ship (which matters more with real users and store updates, W22, where version history and release notes are part of the process). This is the difference between a *prototype* (works, but built quickly, hard to maintain) and a *professional* codebase (typed, tested, organized, documented, *built to last and grow*). For Hydra, the v0.4 cleanup completes its transformation from a quickly-built v0.1-0.3 into a *solid, maintainable, professional* codebase, ready to *grow* into the real, complex app the rest of the track builds (more screens, native features, backend, polish, distribution). The takeaway is that *engineering maturity, quality tooling (types, tests, lint, format), good architecture (organization, separation, reusability, consistency), and documentation (CHANGELOG)*, is what makes a codebase *sustainable* as it grows, and v0.4 establishes all of it for Hydra. This foundation pays off across the rest of the track, as Hydra grows, the v0.4-established maturity (typed, tested, organized) keeps it *maintainable* rather than collapsing into mess. Paying off the technical debt and building the maturity foundation *now* is what enables the app's future growth.

weeks.title: Forms, Inputs, and Keyboard Handling
weeks.context:
Forms and keyboard handling are where most mobile apps fall apart. On web, a form is straightforward, the browser handles keyboard appearance and the page scrolls automatically. On mobile, the keyboard covers half the screen, can obscure the active input, and has OS-specific behaviour (auto-capitalisation, auto-correct, return key labelling). Getting forms right on mobile is a skill that takes explicit attention.

TextInput is the React Native input component. Its props control every aspect of keyboard and input behaviour: keyboardType ('numeric', 'email-address', 'phone-pad'), autoCapitalize ('none', 'words', 'sentences'), autoCorrect (disable for usernames, email), returnKeyType ('next', 'done', 'search'), secureTextEntry (for passwords), autoFocus (focus on mount). Ignoring these makes your forms feel unpolished.

KeyboardAvoidingView is the component that moves content up when the keyboard appears. It has platform-specific behaviour: on iOS, use behavior='padding'; on Android, use behavior='height'. Often combined with ScrollView so the user can scroll through the form. For simple forms (2-3 fields), a single KeyboardAvoidingView with padding is fine. For longer forms, nest inside a ScrollView.

Focus management: the user should be able to Tab (or press Next on the keyboard) through fields in order without lifting their fingers from the keyboard. Implement this by calling ref.current.focus() on the next field when the user presses the return key (onSubmitEditing on each TextInput calls focus on the next ref). The last field's returnKeyType is 'done' and its onSubmitEditing submits the form.

Form validation: validate on submit (shows errors all at once when the user finishes filling in the form) or validate on blur (shows an error when the user leaves a field). Validate-on-submit is less intrusive. Validate-on-blur for fields with specific format requirements (email, password strength). Never validate while the user is typing, it is annoying and often wrong (an email address is technically invalid while you are typing it).

react-hook-form is the standard library for form state management in React Native. It handles field registration, validation, error messages, and submission with minimal re-renders.

[CODE] STEP 1, Install `react-hook-form`, `zod`, and `@hookform/resolvers`.

weeks.title: Animations and Gestures, Where Mobile Feels Native
weeks.context:
Animations and gestures are what separate apps that feel native from apps that feel like a website wrapped in a shell. On the web, animation is an enhancement. On mobile, it is part of the interaction model, the swipe to dismiss, the spring when you release a dragged element, the haptic tap on confirmation. Users feel the quality of your animations even when they cannot articulate it.

React Native Animated API is the built-in animation system. It works by driving native values that never cross the JavaScript bridge during animation, the animation runs on the UI thread. The key: Animated.Value is a mutable container, not a regular number. You connect it to component styles via Animated.View. You drive it with Animated.timing (linear/easing-based), Animated.spring (physics-based, bouncy), or Animated.decay (drag-and-release friction). Always use useNativeDriver: true when animating opacity and transform properties, it moves the animation to the GPU and keeps it smooth even when JavaScript is busy.

react-native-reanimated 2+ is the modern animation library. It moves animation logic to a worklet, a tiny JavaScript function that runs on the UI thread, not the main JavaScript thread. This means animations stay smooth even during heavy JavaScript work (network requests, complex state updates). The Shared Value (useSharedValue) is reanimated's equivalent of Animated.Value. useAnimatedStyle derives animated styles from shared values. runOnJS allows you to call a JavaScript function from a worklet when needed.

react-native-gesture-handler replaces React Native's default gesture system with a more powerful one that runs on the native thread. GestureDetector with Gesture.Pan(), Gesture.Tap(), Gesture.Pinch() gives you multi-gesture support and proper gesture priority. Combined with reanimated, this is the stack used in the most polished apps.

This week you add three animations to Hydra: a spring animation when a habit is checked off (the checkmark bounces in), a swipe-to-delete gesture on habit rows, and a smooth tab transition.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: What is the difference between useNativeDriver: true and false in React Native Animated, and why does it matter? useNativeDriver: true tells the Animated system to serialise the animation configuration and send it to the native thread once. The animation then runs entirely on the native thread without any communication back to JavaScript until it completes. This means even if the JavaScript thread is busy (loading data, running a reducer), the animation plays at 60fps. useNativeDriver: false runs the animation on the JavaScript thread, on every animation frame, JavaScript computes the new value and updates the component. Any JavaScript work pauses the animation. The constraint: useNativeDriver only works for opacity and transform. Width, height, and colour cannot use the native driver.

weeks.title: Theming, Dark Mode, and Design Systems
weeks.context:
Design systems on mobile are about consistency and speed. Every screen should feel like it belongs to the same app, same spacing scale, same colour palette, same typography, same component behaviour. A design system is not just a style guide document; it is code: a set of base components that enforce the system and make it impossible to accidentally use a spacing value that is not on the scale.

Dark mode on iOS and Android is user-controlled at the OS level. Users expect your app to respect their preference. React Native's useColorScheme hook returns 'light' or 'dark' based on the OS setting. A good dark mode is not just inverting colours, dark backgrounds should be very dark grey (#121212 or #1C1C1E) not pure black (#000000), and text should be slightly off-white (#E1E1E1) not pure white (#FFFFFF). Pure black on pure white feels harsh.

Theming architecture: define your design tokens as a TypeScript object, colours, spacing, typography, border radii. Create a light theme and a dark theme. Expose the current theme via a React context (ThemeContext) so any component can access it. Many teams use a custom hook: const { colors, spacing } = useTheme(). The alternative is a theming library, react-native-paper or NativeWind (Tailwind for React Native).

Typography: mobile apps should have a small, coherent set of text styles. Define them explicitly: header (24px, bold), title (18px, semibold), body (14px, regular), caption (12px, regular). Apply them via a Text component that accepts a variant prop. The OS handles the base font, San Francisco on iOS, Roboto on Android. If you need a custom font, use expo-font. Keep it to two weights maximum, loading many font files increases startup time.

Spacing scale: use multiples of 4 or 8 as your spacing unit. spacing.xs = 4, spacing.sm = 8, spacing.md = 16, spacing.lg = 24, spacing.xl = 32. Never use arbitrary values like padding: 13, it breaks the visual rhythm. Standardising spacing is the single highest-impact thing you can do for visual consistency without a designer.

weeks.title: Local Storage, AsyncStorage, MMKV, SQLite
weeks.context:
Data that does not persist across app restarts is data the user has to re-enter. Local storage is how mobile apps remember state. There are three levels of local storage, each with different characteristics, and choosing the wrong one for your use case causes performance problems or data loss.

AsyncStorage is a simple key-value store backed by the device's file system. It is asynchronous (reads and writes are non-blocking I/O operations). It stores strings, you JSON.stringify objects before storing and JSON.parse after reading. It has no schema, no queries, and no transactions. Appropriate for: small amounts of configuration data (user preferences, theme setting, reminder time), simple flags (has the user seen the onboarding?). Not appropriate for: large datasets, structured data you want to query, data that updates frequently.

MMKV is a key-value store that works via memory-mapped files, reads are synchronous (no await required) and extremely fast (microseconds vs milliseconds). It uses the same API pattern as AsyncStorage but synchronously. Install via expo-community-flipper or react-native-mmkv. Appropriate for: same use cases as AsyncStorage, but where synchronous access is important (accessing values inside gesture handlers or worklets) or where you have many small reads.

SQLite is a relational database embedded in your app. It supports SQL queries, indexes, transactions, foreign keys, and can handle millions of rows efficiently. Reads and writes are asynchronous. Covered in W3. Appropriate for: structured data you need to query (habit history, order history, cached API responses).

Secure storage: AsyncStorage and MMKV store data in plaintext on the device. For sensitive data (auth tokens, API keys, biometric-protected secrets), use expo-secure-store, which uses iOS Keychain and Android Keystore, OS-level secure enclaves. Always store user credentials and tokens in secure storage.

This week you audit Hydra's storage: move all simple settings to MMKV (synchronous, fast), keep the completion history in SQLite, and move the auth token (if you add authentication) to expo-secure-store.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You are storing a user auth token after login. It should persist across app restarts but should not be readable by other apps or accessible if the device is rooted. Which storage layer do you use and why? expo-secure-store. On iOS, it stores values in the Keychain, an OS-managed secure enclave that is inaccessible to other apps and survives app reinstalls (unless you delete it). On Android, it uses the Keystore system with encryption at rest. AsyncStorage and MMKV store data in plaintext in the app's sandbox, accessible to anyone who can read the device's storage (rooted devices, adb backup). Tokens are credentials, they get the most secure storage available.

weeks.title: Camera, Photos, and Media Capture
weeks.context:
The camera is the most personal sensor on a mobile device. Camera and media capture features are what make mobile apps feel like mobile apps, not just web pages in a container. Permissions, preview, capture, processing: these are the four phases of every camera interaction.

expo-camera provides a camera preview component that shows the live camera feed. expo-image-picker provides the simpler flow: the OS camera app opens, the user takes the photo, the result (a URI) is returned to your app. Use expo-image-picker when you want the standard OS camera experience. Use expo-camera when you need a custom camera UI (overlays, real-time filters, barcode scanning in your own UI).

Permissions: camera access requires explicit user permission on both iOS and Android. Request with Camera.requestCameraPermissionsAsync(). On iOS, the permission dialog text is set in your app.json (ios.infoPlist.NSCameraUsageDescription). If denied, you must direct the user to Settings. The UX pattern is the same as notifications: explain why before requesting.

Media library access: after capturing, you may want to save to the user's photo library. This requires a separate permission: MediaLibrary.requestPermissionsAsync(). On iOS 14+, the user can grant access to specific photos, not the entire library, your picker gets a selection from what the user allows.

Image processing: captured images are full-resolution (12MP on modern phones, multi-megabyte files). You almost never want to upload a full-resolution image to your server. Process before upload: resize using expo-image-manipulator, compress to reduce file size, convert to JPEG or WebP. A 300KB processed image is fine for most use cases; a 8MB original is not.

The barcode scanner use case: expo-camera has a built-in barcode scanner. Set onBarcodeScanned prop and the camera fires a callback with the barcode data when it detects one. This enables QR code scanning, product barcode scanning, and any scan-to-action flow, with no external library.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: What is the difference between expo-camera and expo-image-picker, and when do you use each? expo-image-picker opens the OS native picker, either the camera app (launchCameraAsync) or the photo library (launchImageLibraryAsync). The OS handles the UI entirely. The result is a URI to the selected/captured image. Use it when you want the standard platform camera experience: simple, reliable, no custom UI. expo-camera renders a CameraView component inside your own UI. You control the frame, overlays, buttons, and capture logic. Use it when you need a custom camera experience: a barcode scanner with an overlay, a photo booth with a timer, a document scanner with edge detection.

weeks.title: Location, Maps, and Geofencing
weeks.context:
Location is the feature that makes mobile apps contextually aware. A restaurant app knows you are near a restaurant. A fitness app tracks your run. A delivery app shows you where the driver is. Location on mobile has two modes: foreground (the app is open and active) and background (the app is in the background or not running). They have different capabilities, different battery impacts, and different permission requirements.

expo-location provides the location API. Foreground location: requestForegroundPermissionsAsync() and getCurrentPositionAsync() or watchPositionAsync(). Background location: requestBackgroundPermissionsAsync() (a separate, stricter permission) and startLocationUpdatesAsync() (requires a background task). Always start with foreground, background location requires explicit user approval and App Store justification.

Accuracy levels matter for battery. Accuracy.Balanced uses cell towers and Wi-Fi, fast, low battery drain, accuracy of ~100 metres. Accuracy.High uses GPS, slower to acquire, significant battery drain, accuracy of ~5 metres. Accuracy.BestForNavigation uses GPS with additional sensors, maximum accuracy, maximum battery drain. Use Balanced for most cases. Only use High or BestForNavigation when navigation or precise tracking is required.

Maps: react-native-maps is the standard. On iOS it renders Apple Maps. On Android it renders Google Maps (requires a Google Maps API key). You place MapView as a full-screen component, add Marker components for points of interest, and Polyline for routes.

Geofencing: trigger code when the user enters or exits a geographic region (a circle defined by latitude, longitude, and radius). expo-location has startGeofencingAsync, it monitors regions in the background and fires a background task. Use case: notify the user when they are near a Bean Forge coffee shop, check in automatically when a runner passes a checkpoint.

Geocoding: convert addresses to coordinates (forward geocoding) and coordinates to addresses (reverse geocoding). expo-location has reverseGeocodeAsync(coords) which returns a structured address object. For forward geocoding (address to coordinates), use the Google Geocoding API or expo-location's geocodeAsync.

items.body: A fitness app wants to track a user's run continuously in the foreground. The user starts a run, locks their phone, and keeps running. After 5 minutes, the app stops receiving location updates. What is happening and how do you fix it? When the user locks the phone, your app moves to the background. Foreground location (watchPositionAsync) stops when the app is backgrounded. To track location during a locked screen, you need background location: requestBackgroundPermissionsAsync() and startLocationUpdatesAsync() with a TaskManager background task. On iOS, you must also add UIBackgroundModes: location to your app.json. This requires App Store Review justification, you must clearly describe why background location is needed.

weeks.title: Push Notifications, The Right Way
weeks.context:
Push notifications are the most powerful re-engagement tool in mobile. Done right, they bring users back to your app at the right moment with the right message. Done wrong, they are spam that makes users disable notifications or uninstall the app. The right way: use them sparingly, make every notification relevant to the individual user, and give users control over what they receive.

There are two types of notifications. Local notifications (covered in W2) are scheduled by the app and delivered by the OS without a network request. Push notifications (this week) originate from a server, are delivered through Apple Push Notification service (APNs) on iOS and Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) on Android, and arrive even when the app is not running.

Expo Push Notification Service (EPNS) is the simplest path. It abstracts APNs and FCM behind a single API. Your server sends a POST request to Expo's push endpoint with the Expo Push Token and the message payload. Expo routes it to the correct platform service. You do not need to configure APNs or FCM certificates during development, Expo handles it. In production (when you submit to the App Store), you configure the certificates in Expo's dashboard.

Expo Push Token: a unique identifier for a specific app install on a specific device. Get it with Notifications.getExpoPushTokenAsync(). Store it on your server associated with the user. When you want to send a notification to a user, look up their push token and send to it.

Notification handling: when a notification arrives, your app may be in three states. Foreground (app open and active): the OS does not show a system notification; you handle it in your app's notification listener. Background (app not active): the OS shows the notification; tapping it brings the app to the foreground. Killed (app not running): the OS shows the notification; tapping it launches the app.

Deep linking via notifications: the notification payload can include data (a JSON object). When the user taps the notification, your app receives this data. Use it to navigate to the specific screen relevant to the notification, a new message, an order update, a friend request.

weeks.title: Native Modules, When JavaScript Isn't Enough
weeks.context:
React Native runs JavaScript, but most device capabilities (camera, Bluetooth, NFC, advanced sensors) are implemented in native code. Native modules are the bridge between JavaScript and native APIs, they expose native functionality as JavaScript functions. Most of the time, you use pre-built native modules from the Expo SDK or the React Native community. Sometimes, you need to write one yourself.

The old native module API required writing separate implementations in Objective-C/Swift (iOS) and Java/Kotlin (Android), then writing a JavaScript wrapper. The new React Native Architecture uses JSI (JavaScript Interface), native modules register C++ functions that can be called directly from JavaScript without the asynchronous bridge. This is faster and synchronous.

Expo Modules API is the recommended way to write native modules for Expo projects. It provides a TypeScript-first API that generates the boilerplate and handles the bridge. You write the native code (Swift/Kotlin) and the TypeScript interface; Expo Modules handles the wiring. An Expo module is a local package in your project, not a separate npm package.

When you do NOT need a custom native module: most hardware interactions are covered by Expo SDKs. Before writing native code, search the Expo SDK, the React Native community packages, and expo.dev/packages. Expo's managed APIs cover: camera, location, sensors, notifications, secure storage, biometrics, haptics, audio, video, network, brightness, and many more.

When you DO need a custom native module: you need a third-party SDK that only provides a native library (a Bluetooth hardware SDK, a proprietary payment terminal SDK, a specific enterprise MDM integration). Or you need to squeeze performance out of a computation that is too slow in JavaScript. Or you need synchronous access to a native API that only supports async in the available modules.

This week: you write a small Expo Module that exposes the native device battery API, not because you need it (expo-battery covers this), but to understand the pattern. Then you integrate an existing native library.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: What is the React Native bridge and what are its performance limitations? The bridge is a serialised, asynchronous, batched channel between JavaScript and native code. Every native call is serialised to JSON, sent across the bridge, deserialised, executed, the result serialised and sent back. This round trip takes microseconds in the best case but the serialisation overhead means you cannot call native functions thousands of times per second. The bridge is also asynchronous, you cannot synchronously read a native value and use it in the same JavaScript expression. JSI (the new architecture) replaces the bridge with direct C++ function calls, synchronous, faster, no serialisation.

weeks.title: Networking, APIs, Offline, Sync
weeks.context:
Mobile apps live on unreliable networks. Cellular connections drop in tunnels. Users switch between Wi-Fi and 4G. A user in a rural area might have 2G for an hour. Your app must degrade gracefully when the network is unavailable and catch up when it returns. An app that shows a blank screen when offline is not a production app.

Network state detection: expo-network provides NetInfo.fetch() and NetInfo.addEventListener for network state changes. But detecting "connected to Wi-Fi" does not mean the internet is actually reachable, the user might be connected to a hotel Wi-Fi with a captive portal. A real connectivity check pings a known server.

Optimistic updates: when the user takes an action (checks off a habit, sends a message), update the UI immediately without waiting for the server response. Then send the network request in the background. If it fails, roll back the UI change and show an error. This makes the app feel instant even on slow networks.

Request queuing: for actions taken offline (the user adds a habit while on a plane), queue the request and execute it when connectivity returns. expo-task-manager with a background fetch can process the queue when the app is in the background.

Caching API responses: for data that does not change frequently (menu items, user profile), cache the last successful response locally. When the app loads, show the cached data immediately while fetching fresh data in the background. This is the stale-while-revalidate pattern, the app never shows a blank loading state.

react-query (also called TanStack Query) is the standard library for server state management in React Native. It handles: caching, background refetching, deduplication (multiple components requesting the same data get one request), optimistic updates, error boundaries, and offline support. It replaces most of the custom networking code you would otherwise write.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have a query that fetches the user's habits from the server. The user opens the app with no internet connection. What does the user see? With react-query and a cache: the cached result from the last successful fetch, immediately. The query re-fires (status: 'loading' but data is available from the cache), fails silently (isFetching: true, isError: true, but data still shows), and the UI shows stale data with an optional indicator that it could not refresh. Without a cache: a loading spinner, then an error state. The difference in user experience is significant, cached data gives the user something to work with even offline.

weeks.title: Authentication on Mobile, OAuth, Biometrics, Sessions
weeks.context:
Authentication on mobile has unique challenges compared to the web. There is no browser cookie jar. Sessions must be stored securely. The user expects to stay logged in for weeks or months without being asked to re-authenticate. And mobile adds capabilities the web does not have: biometric authentication (Face ID, Touch ID, fingerprint) as a convenient and secure unlock mechanism.

Token storage: after a successful login, you receive an access token (short-lived, e.g., 15 minutes) and a refresh token (long-lived, e.g., 30 days). Store both in expo-secure-store (iOS Keychain, Android Keystore). Never store them in AsyncStorage or MMKV (plaintext). The access token goes in the Authorization header of every API request. The refresh token is used to get a new access token when the current one expires.

Axios interceptors: configure an Axios instance with a request interceptor that adds the Authorization header, and a response interceptor that detects 401 responses, refreshes the token, and retries the original request. The user never knows the token was refreshed, they stay logged in transparently.

OAuth on mobile uses the device browser (not a WebView) for the OAuth flow. This is a security requirement, WebViews allow the app to read the credentials the user enters, defeating the purpose of OAuth. expo-auth-session handles this: it opens the system browser for the OAuth flow and uses a deep link to return the authorization code to your app. Configure your app's URL scheme in app.json.

Biometric authentication is not a replacement for your primary auth, it is a local unlock mechanism. The user's credentials (password or token) live in secure storage. When they open the app, instead of showing a login screen, you show a "Unlock with Face ID" prompt. If they authenticate with biometrics, you read the token from secure storage and use it. If biometrics fail or are unavailable, fall back to password.

Session management: decide when the user should be logged out. Options: never log out (refresh token rotates on use, revoke on explicit logout), log out after N days of inactivity (track lastActiveAt), log out when the app is uninstalled (secure store persists across reinstalls on iOS unless you clear it, decide whether you want this behaviour).

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A user's access token expires while they are in the middle of using the app. How does the Axios interceptor handle this transparently? The interceptor catches the 401 response. It calls the refresh token endpoint with the stored refresh token. If the refresh succeeds, it gets a new access token, stores it in secure store, and retries the original request with the new token. From the user's perspective, the request that failed with 401 completes successfully a few hundred milliseconds later, they see no error. If the refresh fails (refresh token expired), the interceptor clears the stored tokens and redirects to the login screen.

weeks.title: Background Tasks and Local Notifications
weeks.context:
Background tasks on mobile are heavily restricted. The operating system aggressively kills background processes to preserve battery life. Understanding what you can and cannot do in the background is essential for building features that work reliably.

iOS background modes: apps can run in the background for specific, declared purposes: audio playback, location updates, background fetch, push content (VoIP, remote notifications with content-available). You declare these in app.json (UIBackgroundModes). Background fetch is the most generally useful, iOS allocates a short window (30 seconds) for your app to run when the OS decides to (typically when the device is charging, on Wi-Fi, and other apps are not actively using resources). You cannot control when this fires.

Android background tasks: more permissive than iOS but increasingly restricted in newer versions. WorkManager (the recommended Android background API) schedules deferrable, guaranteed background work. It respects battery optimisation, runs on device idle when connected to power, and guarantees execution even if the device reboots.

expo-task-manager wraps both platforms' background task systems. You define tasks with TaskManager.defineTask and trigger them with BackgroundFetch.registerTaskAsync (periodic) or Location.startGeofencingAsync (location-triggered). Tasks must complete within the allotted time.

Local notifications as background substitutes: for many "background task" use cases, scheduled local notifications are more reliable. Instead of running background code to check a condition and then show a notification, pre-schedule the notification at a known time. The OS delivers it without waking your app. For reminders (the W2 case), this is always the right approach.

Background fetch realistic expectations: iOS decides when to run background fetch. It uses adaptive scheduling based on how often your app's background fetch updates content that the user then accesses. If users frequently open the app right after a background fetch, iOS schedules it more often. If not, it schedules rarely or never. Do not build features that depend on reliable background fetch timing.

items.body: You want to sync Hydra's habit completions to a server every hour in the background. Can you rely on expo-background-fetch for this? No. Background fetch is unreliable for scheduled, time-critical tasks. iOS decides when to run it based on its own heuristics, it may run every hour or once a day. If the sync fails (offline), queue it locally (SQLite with a synced=false flag) and retry when the app next comes to the foreground (AppState active event). Background fetch can be used as an opportunistic sync to catch anything missed, but not as the primary sync mechanism.

weeks.title: Analytics, Crash Reporting, and Observability
weeks.context:
Mobile analytics and crash reporting are not optional for a production app. Without them, you find out about crashes from App Store reviews, and you find out about user behaviour patterns when you guess. With them, you have evidence.

Crash reporting: Sentry is the standard. It captures unhandled JavaScript errors, native crashes (in development builds), the stack trace, the device model and OS version, the user's session, and groups duplicate crashes. One crash affecting 500 users appears as one Sentry issue with a count of 500. Without Sentry, it looks like no reported bugs. Install @sentry/react-native and initialise it before your root component renders.

Analytics: you need to know how users move through your app. Which screens do they visit? Where do they drop off in the onboarding flow? What features do the retained users use? Mixpanel, Amplitude, or PostHog are the standard mobile analytics tools. You instrument events manually: track('habit_checked', { habitId, habitName, completionStreak }). The events you do not instrument are invisible. Instrument the most important user actions on day one, not later.

Event taxonomy: design your events deliberately before you start tracking. Events have a verb-noun format: habit_completed, habit_created, habit_deleted, onboarding_completed, reminder_set, notification_opened. Include properties that allow segmentation: which habit, what time of day, what device, what app version. An event with no properties tells you something happened but not why or in what context.

Performance monitoring: track app startup time, screen render time, and API response times. Sentry's performance monitoring and Expo's built-in performance tools measure these. App startup time directly affects Day 1 retention, apps that take more than 3 seconds to show content lose a measurable percentage of new users.

Privacy and consent: analytics tracking requires user consent in the EU (GDPR) and increasingly in other jurisdictions. On iOS 14.5+, ATT (App Tracking Transparency) requires explicit user permission for cross-app tracking. For first-party analytics (tracking your own users in your own app), ATT does not apply. But if you use advertising networks or cross-device tracking, ATT consent is required.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Sentry shows an unhandled promise rejection from an API call. The error is "Network request failed" and it has happened 1,847 times in the last week, affecting 234 unique users. How do you investigate this? Check the Sentry issue for the breadcrumbs (the sequence of events before the crash), which screen was the user on? Which API endpoint was failing? Look at the OS distribution, is this only on Android, or both platforms? Check the network timeline, was this during a period when your backend had an incident? Filter by app version, did this start after a specific release? With this information: if it is a specific API endpoint, look at your server logs for that period. If it is all networks equally, check whether the API URL is correct in that version. If it is only Android, check for Android-specific network configuration.

weeks.title: Building for Performance, Bundles, Frames, Memory
weeks.context:
60 frames per second is the contract between your app and your users. At 60fps, animations feel smooth and interactions feel instant. At 30fps, everything feels slightly sluggish. Below 30fps, the app feels broken. Performance problems on mobile have different causes than on web, and fixing them requires understanding how React Native renders.

The render pipeline: React renders to a virtual DOM diff, passes the diff to the React Native bridge (or JSI), which calls native layout and drawing APIs. The result is displayed on screen. This pipeline runs on every state update. The JavaScript thread handles your React renders, event handlers, and business logic. The UI thread handles native rendering. They run concurrently, JavaScript being slow does not directly cause dropped frames, but passing too much work across the bridge can.

The most common performance problems: re-rendering components that did not change, computing expensive values on every render, rendering large lists inefficiently, and passing large data across the bridge too frequently.

React DevTools profiler: shows which components re-rendered and how long each render took. Accessible via the Expo Dev Tools. Use it to identify the "hot" components, the ones that re-render most often and take the longest.

Memoisation: React.memo wraps a component and only re-renders when its props change (shallow equality check). useMemo caches the result of a computation and only recomputes when dependencies change. useCallback caches a function reference and only creates a new function when dependencies change. Overusing these adds complexity, use them only when the React Profiler shows that a component is re-rendering unnecessarily and the re-render is expensive.

FlatList optimisations: getItemLayout tells FlatList the exact height of each item, so it does not need to measure them. initialNumToRender controls how many items render on the first pass. windowSize controls how many screens of content are rendered above and below the visible area. removeClippedSubviews offloads off-screen items from memory (experimental, may cause issues, test carefully).

Hermes is the JavaScript engine used in modern React Native. It is optimised for mobile: it compiles JavaScript to bytecode at build time (instead of JIT at runtime), which significantly reduces startup time. It is enabled by default in Expo SDK 47+.

## Native vs JS performance

60 frames per second is the contract between your app and your users. At 60fps, animations feel smooth and interactions feel instant. At 30fps, everything feels slightly sluggish. The render pipeline: React renders to a virtual DOM diff, passes the diff to the React Native bridge (or JSI), which calls native layout and drawing APIs

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have a HabitList component that re-renders every second because a parent component has a timer that updates every second. The timer is needed in the parent for a countdown display. The HabitList does not use the timer at all. How do you stop HabitList from re-rendering? Wrap HabitList in React.memo. React.memo does a shallow equality check on props. If the HabitList's props (habits, onToggle) did not change, it skips re-rendering even when the parent re-renders. Ensure the onToggle function is wrapped in useCallback so it has a stable reference, if it is a new function on every render, React.memo sees changed props and re-renders anyway.

weeks.title: Accessibility, Building for Everyone
weeks.context:
Mobile accessibility is about building apps that work for the 15-20% of users who have visual, motor, or cognitive disabilities. Screen readers, large text, reduced motion, and switch access are not edge cases, they are features that millions of users depend on daily. App stores increasingly require accessibility compliance, and enterprise app buyers evaluate it in their procurement criteria.

VoiceOver (iOS) and TalkBack (Android) are the built-in screen readers. They read aloud the content and purpose of every UI element as the user navigates with swipe gestures (or on Android, touch exploration). A properly accessible app works completely eyes-free. Test your app with VoiceOver enabled (iOS: Settings > Accessibility > VoiceOver > On, or triple-click the side button). Navigate using swipe right/left to move between elements, double-tap to activate.

The accessibility API in React Native: accessible={true} marks an element as a single accessible unit. accessibilityLabel="Check off morning run" provides the text VoiceOver reads. accessibilityHint="Double tap to check or uncheck" provides additional context. accessibilityRole="button" tells the screen reader what type of element it is ('button', 'checkbox', 'header', 'image', 'text', 'link'). accessibilityState={{ checked: isCompleted }} communicates state.

Accessible names: if an element has only an icon (no text label), it is invisible to screen readers without an accessibilityLabel. A button with a trash icon and no label is announced as "image" or nothing. Add accessibilityLabel="Delete habit" to icon-only buttons.

Text scaling: users set a preferred text size in OS settings. On iOS, this affects all apps that use Dynamic Type. React Native Text components scale with system font size by default. Test at the largest text size (Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Larger Text > max). Layout must not break, buttons must stay tappable, text must not be clipped.

Reduced motion: some users experience vestibular disorders and get motion sickness from animations. iOS and Android have a "Reduce Motion" setting. Read it with AccessibilityInfo.isReduceMotionEnabled() and disable or simplify animations for these users.

weeks.title: Internationalisation, Multiple Languages, Currencies, Dates
weeks.context:
Internationalisation (i18n) is preparing your app to support multiple languages, regions, and locales. Localisation (l10n) is adapting the app for a specific locale. Most apps need both if they are targeting international markets. Even for English-only apps, you should understand date, number, and currency formatting differences.

i18n-js and i18next are the standard libraries. They manage translation strings, handle pluralisation rules (English: 1 item, 2 items; Arabic: has 6 plural forms), interpolate variables into translated strings, and fall back to a default language when a translation is missing.

Translation files: you maintain one JSON file per locale, with the same key structure. en.json: { "habit_count": "{{count}} habits" }, ar.json: { "habit_count": "{{count}} عادة" }. Your code references keys, never hardcoded strings: t('habit_count', { count: habits.length }).

Locale detection: on mobile, the device locale (the language/region the user has set in their OS settings) is available from expo-localization. Expo.getLocales() returns an ordered list of the user's preferred locales. Use the first one as your app's locale if it is supported, otherwise fall back to your default.

Number and currency formatting: 1,234.56 in the US is 1.234,56 in Germany and 1 234,56 in France. Use Intl.NumberFormat (built into the JavaScript engine) with the locale: new Intl.NumberFormat('de-DE', { style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR' }).format(1234.56). Never hardcode number separators.

Date and time formatting: July 4 is 4 Juli in German, 4 luglio in Italian. Use Intl.DateTimeFormat for localised date strings. Also consider: some locales use right-to-left (RTL) text direction, Arabic, Hebrew, Persian. React Native has RTL support (I18nManager.forceRTL) but it requires testing and thoughtful layout decisions (margins and paddings swap, icon positions swap, text alignment changes).
